intro: Wedged between the Blackstairs Mountains and the fertile valley of the River Barrow, Carlow is Ireland's second-smallest county, yet it punches well above its size in history. Granite from its uplands built much of Leinster, and the county's ancient nickname, the Dolmen County, comes from the Browneshill portal tomb outside Carlow town, whose colossal capstone is reckoned the heaviest in Europe. The Barrow, Ireland's second-longest river, threads the county from north to south, and its towpath, once walked by horses hauling grain barges to Waterford port, is now one of the country's loveliest long-distance trails.

Carlow town grew rich on milling and malting, and in 1926 it became the home of the Irish Free State's first sugar beet factory, an industry that shaped local farming for seventy years. The county has a strong scholarly streak too: Carlow College, founded in the 1780s, is among the oldest Catholic institutions of higher learning in Ireland, and the town now hosts a campus of the South East Technological University. For visitors tracing roots, the graveyards of Leighlinbridge, St Mullins and Clonegal sit in some of the most tranquil river scenery in the country.

towns.name: Carlow
towns.note: The county town on the Barrow, home to Carlow College, the Delta Sensory Gardens and the ruins of a 13th-century Norman castle.

towns.name: Tullow
towns.note: A market town on the Slaney known as the gateway to the Blackstairs and the home club of rugby star Sean O'Brien, the Tullow Tank.

towns.name: Bagenalstown
towns.note: Officially Muine Bheag, an elegant planned town founded by Walter Bagenal, who intended it to be a Versailles on the Barrow.

towns.name: Borris
towns.note: A handsome Georgian estate village beneath Mount Leinster, seat of the MacMurrough Kavanaghs and famed for its 16-arch railway viaduct.

towns.name: Leighlinbridge
towns.note: A Barrow-side village with one of Ireland's earliest Norman castles and the birthplace of physicist John Tyndall.

towns.name: St Mullins
towns.note: A riverside monastic settlement founded by St Moling, burial place of the kings of Leinster including Art MacMurrough Kavanagh.

towns.name: Clonegal
towns.note: A picture-postcard village at the end of the Wicklow Way, home to the atmospheric 17th-century Huntington Castle.

towns.name: Rathvilly
towns.note: A trim village under Mount Leinster that has repeatedly won Ireland's Tidy Towns competition.

towns.name: Hacketstown
towns.note: A hillside town near the Wicklow border, ancestral home of the family of 1916-era patriot Kevin Barry.

towns.name: Myshall
towns.note: A quiet village at the foot of Mount Leinster, birthplace of American publishing magnate Peter Fenelon Collier.

people.name: John Tyndall
people.note: The Leighlinbridge-born physicist who explained why the sky is blue and was a pioneer in understanding the greenhouse effect.

people.name: William Dargan
people.note: Born near Carlow town in 1799, the great engineer who built most of Ireland's early railways and funded the exhibition that led to the National Gallery.

people.name: Saoirse Ronan
people.note: The four-time Oscar-nominated actress who grew up in Ardattin, near Tullow, and has often spoken of her Carlow childhood.

people.name: Myles Keogh
people.note: A soldier from Leighlinbridge who fought for the Pope and the Union Army before dying with Custer at Little Bighorn in 1876.

people.name: Samuel Haughton
people.note: A Carlow-born polymath of Trinity College who made contributions to geology, medicine and mathematics in the 19th century.

people.name: Sean O'Brien
people.note: The Tullow-born flanker who won multiple Six Nations titles with Ireland and toured with the British and Irish Lions.

people.name: Peter Fenelon Collier
people.note: The Myshall emigrant who founded Collier's Weekly, one of America's most influential magazines.

people.name: Patrick Francis Moran
people.note: The Leighlinbridge-born cardinal who became Archbishop of Sydney and a towering figure in Australian Catholic history.

people.name: Kevin Barry
people.note: The 18-year-old medical student executed in 1920, whose family farm was at Tombeagh near Hacketstown, where he spent much of his youth.

facts: The capstone of the Browneshill Dolmen outside Carlow town weighs an estimated 100 tonnes and is widely regarded as the heaviest in Europe.
Carlow was one of the first towns in Ireland or Britain to have electric street lighting, powered from 1891 by a hydroelectric scheme at Milford Mills on the Barrow.
Ireland's first sugar beet factory opened in Carlow in 1926 and operated until 2005, earning the county a central place in Irish agricultural history.
At roughly 897 square kilometres, Carlow is the second-smallest of Ireland's 32 counties, larger only than Louth.
Mount Leinster, on the Carlow-Wexford border, rises to 795 metres and its summit transmitter mast serves much of the south-east.
The Black Castle at Leighlinbridge, begun in 1181, guards one of the oldest bridging points on the River Barrow, with the present bridge dating from 1320.
Carlow College, established in the 1780s and opened in 1793, is one of the oldest centres of Catholic higher education in Ireland.
The Duckett's Grove estate near Carlow town features a dramatic Gothic Revival ruin that has become one of Ireland's most photographed abandoned houses.

intro: Every Irish family story seems to pass through Dublin sooner or later, whether through its tenements, its docks or its emigrant ships. Founded as a Viking trading post around 841 at the dark tidal pool, the Dubh Linn, that gave the city its English name, the capital carries eleven centuries of layered history: medieval Christ Church and Dublin Castle, the grand Georgian squares of the 18th century, the bullet-scarred GPO of 1916, and the glass towers of the modern docklands. In Irish it is Baile Atha Cliath, the town of the hurdled ford, an even older name for an even older crossing of the Liffey.

Dublin's literary pedigree is unmatched for a city of its size: it was designated a UNESCO City of Literature in 2010 and claims Swift, Wilde, Joyce, Shaw, Beckett and Stoker among its own. Beyond the city centre, the county offers real variety, from the fishing harbours of Howth and Skerries to the Victorian seafront of Dun Laoghaire and the beaches of the north county. Today greater Dublin is home to well over a quarter of the Republic's population and hosts the European headquarters of many of the world's biggest technology firms, yet Moore Street traders and Sunday GAA crowds keep its older character alive.

towns.name: Dublin City
towns.note: The capital and largest city in Ireland, straddling the Liffey and home to Trinity College, the GPO and the Guinness brewery at St James's Gate.

towns.name: Howth
towns.note: A fishing village on a rugged peninsula north of the city, famed for its cliff walk, seafood and the 1914 gun-running that armed the Irish Volunteers.

towns.name: Dun Laoghaire
towns.note: A Victorian harbour town with two great granite piers, once the mail-boat gateway to Ireland and the departure point for generations of emigrants.

towns.name: Malahide
towns.note: An affluent seaside town whose castle was held by the Talbot family for nearly 800 years.

towns.name: Swords
towns.note: The county town of Fingal, grown from a 6th-century monastic settlement founded by St Colmcille into one of Ireland's largest towns.

towns.name: Tallaght
towns.note: Once a small village on an ancient monastic site, now the bustling heart of South Dublin with its own hospital, theatre and stadium.

towns.name: Dalkey
towns.note: A medieval heritage town turned upmarket coastal village, with two castles on its main street and a long roll-call of celebrity residents.

towns.name: Skerries
towns.note: A north county fishing town with restored 18th-century mills and islands offshore where St Patrick is said to have landed.

towns.name: Balbriggan
towns.note: A former cotton and hosiery town in north Fingal whose stockings were once famous enough that Queen Victoria wore them.

towns.name: Lucan
towns.note: A Liffey-side village swallowed by the growing city, once celebrated for its spa and its demesne waterfalls.

people.name: James Joyce
people.note: The author of Ulysses, born in Rathgar in 1882, who mapped Dublin so completely he claimed the city could be rebuilt from his pages.

people.name: Oscar Wilde
people.note: The playwright and wit, born on Westland Row in 1854 and raised on Merrion Square, where his statue now reclines.

people.name: Samuel Beckett
people.note: The Nobel laureate author of Waiting for Godot, born in Foxrock in 1906; a Liffey bridge now bears his name.

people.name: George Bernard Shaw
people.note: Born in Portobello in 1856, the only person to win both a Nobel Prize in Literature and an Academy Award.

people.name: Bram Stoker
people.note: The creator of Dracula, born in Clontarf in 1847 and educated at Trinity College while working at Dublin Castle.

people.name: Jonathan Swift
people.note: The satirist behind Gulliver's Travels, born in Dublin in 1667 and later Dean of St Patrick's Cathedral, where he is buried.

people.name: Phil Lynott
people.note: The Thin Lizzy frontman raised in Crumlin, honoured with a bronze statue off Grafton Street.

people.name: Bono
people.note: Born Paul Hewson in Dublin in 1960, the U2 singer who formed the band with schoolmates from Mount Temple Comprehensive.

people.name: Luke Kelly
people.note: The flame-haired Dubliners balladeer from Sheriff Street, whose voice defined songs like Raglan Road and The Auld Triangle.

people.name: Maeve Binchy
people.note: The Dalkey-born novelist whose warm tales of Irish life sold more than 40 million copies worldwide.

facts: Arthur Guinness signed a 9,000-year lease on the St James's Gate brewery in 1759 at an annual rent of 45 pounds.
Handel's Messiah received its world premiere on Fishamble Street in Dublin in April 1742.
Phoenix Park, at around 707 hectares, is one of the largest enclosed urban parks in any European capital and has a resident herd of wild fallow deer.
The Rotunda, founded in 1745, is the oldest continuously operating maternity hospital in the world.
Dublin's English name comes from the Irish Dubh Linn, meaning black pool, a tidal pond where the River Poddle met the Liffey behind Dublin Castle.
Three Nobel laureates in literature were born in Dublin: W.B. Yeats, George Bernard Shaw and Samuel Beckett.
Dublin was designated a UNESCO City of Literature in 2010, one of only a handful of cities then to hold the title.
St Patrick's Cathedral, founded in 1191, is the largest church in Ireland, and Jonathan Swift served as its dean for over 30 years.

intro: Horses and saints have shaped Kildare in equal measure. The county takes its name from Cill Dara, the church of the oak, where St Brigid founded her great double monastery in the 5th century, and her perpetual flame has been rekindled in Kildare town in modern times. Just outside the town stretches the Curragh, a vast unfenced plain of short grass grazed by sheep for millennia and galloped over by racehorses for centuries; all five Irish Classic flat races are run at its racecourse, and the Irish National Stud and Japanese Gardens lie on its edge at Tully.

Flat, fertile and threaded by both the Grand and Royal Canals, Kildare was long the breadbasket and thoroughfare of Leinster, dominated by the FitzGerald earls whose power once rivalled the Crown's. The Bog of Allen spreads across its west, while the east has become Dublin's busiest commuter belt, anchored by Intel's enormous campus at Leixlip and the university town of Maynooth. Celbridge holds Castletown House, Ireland's grandest Palladian mansion, and Athy's Shackleton Museum honours the county's polar explorer son. Few counties blend big-house heritage, working bogland and world-class bloodstock quite so seamlessly.

towns.name: Naas
towns.note: The county town, whose Irish name Nas na Riogh means meeting place of the kings, once a seat of the kings of Leinster.

towns.name: Newbridge
towns.note: Kildare's largest town, built around a 19th-century cavalry barracks and now famous for Newbridge Silverware.

towns.name: Kildare
towns.note: A cathedral town founded on St Brigid's 5th-century monastery, with a climbable round tower and the National Stud on its doorstep.

towns.name: Maynooth
towns.note: A university town containing both Maynooth University and St Patrick's College, once the largest Catholic seminary in the world.

towns.name: Celbridge
towns.note: A Liffey-side town dominated by Castletown House, Ireland's finest Palladian mansion, and the boyhood home of Arthur Guinness.

towns.name: Leixlip
towns.note: A Viking-named town, from the Norse for salmon leap, where Arthur Guinness first brewed and Intel now runs its vast European campus.

towns.name: Athy
towns.note: A Barrow-side market town with a striking Dominican church and a museum devoted to Antarctic explorer Ernest Shackleton.

towns.name: Monasterevin
towns.note: A canal town of bridges and aqueducts once home to poet Gerard Manley Hopkins on his retreats, and to tenor John McCormack at Moore Abbey.

towns.name: Kilcullen
towns.note: A bridge town on the Liffey close to Dun Ailinne, the ancient royal ceremonial site of Leinster.

towns.name: Kilcock
towns.note: A canal-harbour town on the Royal Canal, birthplace of the emigrant poet Teresa Brayton.

people.name: St Brigid
people.note: One of Ireland's three patron saints, who founded her renowned monastery at Kildare around 480 and whose feast day is now a national holiday.

people.name: Arthur Guinness
people.note: The founder of the Guinness brewery, born near Celbridge in 1725, who first brewed at Leixlip before moving to St James's Gate.

people.name: Ernest Shackleton
people.note: The Antarctic explorer, born at Kilkea near Athy in 1874, celebrated for the heroic rescue of his entire Endurance crew.

people.name: Christy Moore
people.note: The folk singer and Planxty and Moving Hearts founder, born and raised in Newbridge.

people.name: Luka Bloom
people.note: The singer-songwriter born Barry Moore in Newbridge, younger brother of Christy Moore.

people.name: John Devoy
people.note: The Fenian organiser from Kill who spent decades in America masterminding support for Irish independence, including the Catalpa rescue.

people.name: Silken Thomas FitzGerald
people.note: The 10th Earl of Kildare, whose dramatic 1534 rebellion against Henry VIII ended the FitzGerald dynasty's dominance and his own life.

people.name: Damien Rice
people.note: The internationally successful singer-songwriter behind the album O, raised in Celbridge.

people.name: Teresa Brayton
people.note: The Kilcock-born poet of the diaspora, best remembered for the emigrant ballad The Old Bog Road.

facts: The Curragh's roughly 2,000 hectares of unfenced short grass form one of the largest areas of semi-natural grassland in Europe, with racing recorded there for centuries.
All five Irish Classic flat races, including the Irish Derby, are run at the Curragh racecourse.
Castletown House in Celbridge, begun in 1722, was the first and is the largest Palladian country house ever built in Ireland.
St Patrick's College, Maynooth, founded in 1795, grew into the largest Catholic seminary in the world during the 19th century.
Leixlip takes its name from the Old Norse for salmon leap, one of the few Irish town names of purely Viking origin.
Intel's Leixlip campus, opened in 1989, is one of the largest private investments in the history of the Irish state.
The Japanese Gardens at Tully, created between 1906 and 1910, are regarded as among the finest of their kind in Europe.
Kildare means church of the oak, from the oak tree beside which St Brigid established her monastery.

intro: For a few extraordinary years in the 1640s, Kilkenny city was effectively the capital of Ireland, seat of the Confederate Catholics who governed much of the island from its Parliament. That medieval swagger never quite left: the city keeps its castle, its 13th-century St Canice's Cathedral with a climbable round tower, its narrow slips and its merchant houses, and it remains the only inland city in the Republic. The local black limestone, polished to a gleam and sold as Kilkenny marble, gave the Marble City its nickname and adorns buildings across the world.

Beyond the city, the Nore and Barrow valleys hold some of Ireland's prettiest estate villages, Inistioge and Graiguenamanagh among them, along with the great Cistercian ruins of Jerpoint Abbey and the fortress-like Kells Priory. Castlecomer's plateau was mined for coal for three centuries, while Callan produced both the founder of the Christian Brothers and the architect of the White House. Above all, Kilkenny means hurling: the Cats have won more All-Ireland senior titles than any other county, and on championship Sundays the black and amber stripes are visible in every parish from Urlingford to Mooncoin.

towns.name: Kilkenny
towns.note: The medieval Marble City on the Nore, dominated by Kilkenny Castle, home of the Butler family for almost 600 years.

towns.name: Callan
towns.note: A historic market town that produced Edmund Ignatius Rice, founder of the Christian Brothers, and White House architect James Hoban.

towns.name: Thomastown
towns.note: A Norman market town on the Nore beside the magnificent ruins of Jerpoint Abbey and the renowned Mount Juliet estate.

towns.name: Castlecomer
towns.note: An estate town on the north Kilkenny plateau where anthracite coal was mined for some 300 years, a story told in its Discovery Park.

towns.name: Graiguenamanagh
towns.note: A Barrow-side boating town built around Duiske Abbey, one of the finest Cistercian foundations in Ireland.

towns.name: Inistioge
towns.note: An impossibly pretty village of tree-lined square and ten-arch bridge, a favourite filming location including for Circle of Friends.

towns.name: Bennettsbridge
towns.note: A Nore-side village that became a hub of Irish craft, home to Nicholas Mosse Pottery in an old flour mill.

towns.name: Ballyragget
towns.note: A north Kilkenny market village with a well-preserved 15th-century Butler tower house.

towns.name: Mooncoin
towns.note: A village in the county's southern tip, immortalised in the ballad The Rose of Mooncoin, Kilkenny's sporting anthem.

towns.name: Freshford
towns.note: A quiet village whose 18th-century church preserves a remarkable 12th-century Hiberno-Romanesque doorway.

people.name: James Hoban
people.note: The architect of the White House in Washington, born near Callan around 1755 and trained in Dublin before emigrating.

people.name: George Berkeley
people.note: The great philosopher of idealism, born at Dysart Castle near Thomastown in 1685, after whom Berkeley, California is named.

people.name: Edmund Ignatius Rice
people.note: The Callan-born founder of the Christian Brothers and Presentation Brothers, whose schools educated generations worldwide.

people.name: Henry Shefflin
people.note: The Ballyhale hurler widely regarded as one of the greatest ever, winner of ten All-Ireland senior medals with Kilkenny.

people.name: DJ Carey
people.note: The Gowran-born hurling forward whose skill made him one of the most celebrated players of the 1990s and 2000s.

people.name: Brian Cody
people.note: The James Stephens clubman who managed Kilkenny to eleven All-Ireland titles across 24 seasons, a record in hurling management.

people.name: Alice Kyteler
people.note: The wealthy Kilkenny moneylender accused in 1324 in one of Europe's earliest recorded witchcraft trials; she escaped, but her maid was burned.

people.name: John Banim
people.note: The Kilkenny-born 19th-century novelist and playwright often called the Scott of Ireland for his Tales by the O'Hara Family.

people.name: Hubert Butler
people.note: The essayist of Maidenhall, Bennettsbridge, whose luminous writing on Ireland and Europe won belated international acclaim.

people.name: Thomas Kilroy
people.note: The Callan-born playwright and novelist, a leading figure in the Field Day movement and author of The Big Chapel.

facts: Kilkenny hold more All-Ireland senior hurling titles than any other county, with 36 championships.

The 1324 trial of Alice Kyteler in Kilkenny was one of the earliest witchcraft prosecutions in Europe, and her servant Petronilla de Meath became the first person burned for heresy-linked witchcraft in Ireland.
The Statutes of Kilkenny, passed in 1366, notoriously attempted to ban the Anglo-Norman colonists from adopting Irish language, law, dress and customs.
From 1642 to 1649 Kilkenny was the seat of the Confederate Catholics of Ireland, making it the de facto capital of much of the country.
Kilkenny marble is not true marble but a local black limestone that takes a high polish, and it gave the Marble City its nickname.
Excavations at Dunmore Cave uncovered evidence linked to a Viking massacre recorded there in 928, along with a hoard of 10th-century coins.
Smithwick's ale was first brewed in Kilkenny in 1710 at the St Francis Abbey site, making it one of Ireland's oldest beer brands.
The round tower at St Canice's Cathedral, built in the 9th century, is one of only a few in Ireland that visitors can still climb.

intro: Few counties carry their history in their name the way Laois does. Known for centuries as Queen's County after Mary Tudor, whose 1556 plantation made it one of the first parts of Ireland formally colonised, it reclaimed its ancient name — from the Loígis tribe — after independence. The county's great symbol is the Rock of Dunamase, a shattered fortress on a limestone outcrop that passed as part of Aoife MacMurrough's dowry to Strongbow and was fought over for centuries. The O'More clan resisted the plantation fiercely from these plains, and their defiance shaped the county's early modern story as much as any settler town did.

Modern Laois is a county of quiet good looks and growing confidence. The Slieve Bloom Mountains rise gently along its western edge, laced with waymarked trails and glens, while the flat farmland of the Great Heath spreads eastward. Handsome estate towns like Abbeyleix and Stradbally speak of its landlord past; Stradbally now hosts Electric Picnic, Ireland's biggest music and arts festival, every autumn. Portlaoise has boomed as a motorway-age commuter hub, and Ballyfin Demesne, a Regency mansion turned hotel, is regularly ranked among the finest in the world. It is a county many drive through — and those who stop tend to be pleasantly surprised.

towns.name: Portlaoise
towns.note: The fast-growing county town, founded as Maryborough in 1557, today a major commuter hub and home to Ireland's high-security prison.

towns.name: Abbeyleix
towns.note: An elegant planned estate town laid out by the de Vesci family, known for its heritage streetscape and Morrissey's, one of Ireland's most famous old pubs.

towns.name: Stradbally
towns.note: A pretty estate village that hosts the Electric Picnic festival each year on the grounds of Stradbally Hall, along with a narrow-gauge steam railway museum.

towns.name: Mountmellick
towns.note: A former Quaker industrial town that gave its name to Mountmellick work, a distinctive style of white-on-white embroidery.

towns.name: Portarlington
towns.note: A border town with Offaly noted for its French Huguenot heritage, still remembered in its street names and annual French Festival.

towns.name: Mountrath
towns.note: A market town at the foot of the Slieve Blooms, historically linked to St Fintan and a gateway to the mountains.

towns.name: Durrow
towns.note: A picturesque estate village on the River Erkina famous for its annual Scarecrow Festival.

towns.name: Rathdowney
towns.note: A tidy town in the south of the county with a strong brewing and agricultural heritage, once home to Perry's Brewery.

towns.name: Timahoe
towns.note: A small village dominated by a 12th-century round tower with a rare and richly carved Romanesque doorway.

towns.name: Ballinakill
towns.note: A heritage village near Abbeyleix known for its Georgian square and the nearby Heywood Gardens, designed by Edwin Lutyens.

people.name: James Fintan Lalor
people.note: Influential Young Ireland writer on land reform, born at Tinakill near Raheen, whose ideas shaped later land agitation and republican thought.

people.name: Kevin O'Higgins
people.note: Free State minister and one of the new state's dominant figures, born in Stradbally and assassinated in 1927.

people.name: Bartholomew Mosse
people.note: Surgeon born in Maryborough (Portlaoise) who founded Dublin's Rotunda, the world's first purpose-built maternity hospital.

people.name: Cecil Day-Lewis
people.note: British Poet Laureate and father of actor Daniel Day-Lewis, born at Ballintubbert near Stradbally in 1904.

people.name: Robert Sheehan
people.note: Portlaoise-born actor known for Love/Hate, Misfits and The Umbrella Academy.

people.name: Zach Tuohy
people.note: Portlaoise man who became one of the most-capped Irish players in Australian Rules history, winning an AFL premiership with Geelong.

people.name: Sue Ramsbottom
people.note: Timahoe native regarded as one of the greatest ladies Gaelic footballers of all time, captaining Laois to the 2001 All-Ireland title.

people.name: Rory Óg O'More
people.note: Sixteenth-century chieftain of the O'More clan who led fierce Gaelic resistance to the plantation of Queen's County.

people.name: John Keegan
people.note: Pre-Famine poet and story collector from near Shanahoe, best remembered for the ballad Caoch the Piper.

facts: Laois is the only county in Ireland that does not border a county with a coastline, making it arguably the most landlocked county on the island.

Until 1922 the county was officially called Queen's County, named for Mary I, and Portlaoise was called Maryborough — one half of the first plantation of Ireland in 1556, alongside King's County (Offaly).
The Rock of Dunamase was part of the dowry of Aoife, daughter of Diarmait Mac Murchada, when she married the Norman leader Strongbow in 1170.
Stradbally hosts Electric Picnic, Ireland's largest music and arts festival, which draws around 70,000 people to the grounds of Stradbally Hall each year.
Mountmellick gave its name to a unique form of white-on-white floral embroidery, Mountmellick work, developed in the Quaker town in the early 19th century.
The round tower at Timahoe is the only one in Ireland with an elaborately carved Romanesque doorway, decorated with human faces and interlaced hair.
Portlaoise is home to the Republic of Ireland's only high-security prison.
Ballyfin Demesne, a restored Regency house in the county, has repeatedly been named among the best hotels in the world since opening in 2011.

intro: Longford rewards the traveller who slows down. One of Ireland's smallest counties, tucked between the Shannon and the drumlins of the north midlands, it was for centuries the Gaelic kingdom of Annaly, ruled by the O'Farrells — a name still everywhere in the county. Its western boundary is the Shannon and the broad waters of Lough Ree, its southern reaches are Goldsmith country, and its bogs concealed one of Irish archaeology's great treasures: the Corlea Trackway, a massive oak road laid across the bog in 148 BC and now displayed where it was found near Kenagh.

For a quiet county, Longford's literary and revolutionary footprint is remarkable. Oliver Goldsmith grew up around Ballymahon; Maria Edgeworth wrote her pioneering novels at Edgeworthstown; Padraic Colum, poet of the Irish revival, was born in Longford town. The 1798 Rebellion ended in tragedy at Ballinamuck, where the Franco-Irish army made its last stand, and General Seán Mac Eoin, the Blacksmith of Ballinalee, made the county famous in the War of Independence. Today the restored St Mel's Cathedral crowns Longford town, and Center Parcs at Ballymahon has brought a new wave of visitors to a county long overlooked.

towns.name: Longford
towns.note: The county town on the River Camlin, dominated by the magnificently restored St Mel's Cathedral and long a garrison and market centre.

towns.name: Granard
towns.note: A hilltop town crowned by one of Ireland's finest Norman mottes, known for its harp festival and as the home of Kitty Kiernan.

towns.name: Edgeworthstown
towns.note: Home of the remarkable Edgeworth family, where novelist Maria Edgeworth lived and wrote Castle Rackrent.

towns.name: Ballymahon
towns.note: A broad-streeted town on the River Inny at the heart of Goldsmith country, with Center Parcs Longford Forest nearby.

towns.name: Lanesborough
towns.note: A gateway town where the Shannon enters Lough Ree, long known for its power station and its hot-water stretch beloved of anglers.

towns.name: Ardagh
towns.note: An award-winning heritage village associated with St Mel, who founded a church here in the fifth century.

towns.name: Newtownforbes
towns.note: An estate village beside Castle Forbes, seat of the Earls of Granard and one of the longest continuously occupied family castles in Ireland.

towns.name: Drumlish
towns.note: A village at the foot of Cairn Hill with strong traditions of country music and emigration.

towns.name: Abbeyshrule
towns.note: A tranquil village on the Inny and the Royal Canal, home to a ruined Cistercian abbey and a well-known small airfield.

towns.name: Kenagh
towns.note: The village closest to the Corlea Trackway visitor centre, where an Iron Age bog road is preserved in situ.

people.name: Oliver Goldsmith
people.note: Author of The Vicar of Wakefield and She Stoops to Conquer, born at Pallas near Ballymahon and reared in the county's south.

people.name: Maria Edgeworth
people.note: Pioneering novelist who spent most of her life at Edgeworthstown, where she wrote Castle Rackrent, often called the first regional novel in English.

people.name: Seán Mac Eoin
people.note: The Blacksmith of Ballinalee, celebrated IRA commander in the War of Independence and later a government minister.

people.name: Kitty Kiernan
people.note: Granard woman famous as the fiancée of Michael Collins, whose letters to her are among the most read documents of the revolutionary era.

people.name: Padraic Colum
people.note: Poet, playwright and folklorist of the Irish literary revival, born in Longford town in 1881.

people.name: Albert Reynolds
people.note: Taoiseach from 1992 to 1994 and a key architect of the Northern Ireland peace process, who built his business empire and political base in Longford.

people.name: Ray Flynn
people.note: Longford-born athlete who has held the Irish mile record since 1982 and became a leading international athletics agent.

people.name: Declan Nerney
people.note: Country music star from Drumlish, one of the best-known figures on the Irish country scene.

people.name: St Mel
people.note: Fifth-century bishop, traditionally a nephew of St Patrick, who founded the church at Ardagh and gave his name to Longford's cathedral.

facts: The Corlea Trackway near Kenagh is a massive Iron Age oak road built in 148 BC — the largest trackway of its kind uncovered in Europe, with an 18-metre stretch preserved under cover where it was found.
The 1798 Rebellion effectively ended at the Battle of Ballinamuck in north Longford, where the combined French and Irish force under General Humbert was finally defeated.
St Mel's Cathedral in Longford town was gutted by fire on Christmas morning 2009 and reopened in 2014 after one of the largest church restoration projects ever undertaken in Ireland.
The county takes its name from the Irish longphort, a fortress or stronghold of the O'Farrells, who ruled the territory as the kingdom of Annaly for centuries.
Maria Edgeworth's Castle Rackrent (1800), written at Edgeworthstown, was admired by Jane Austen and credited by Walter Scott as an inspiration for his own novels.
The Royal Canal completes its 146-kilometre journey from Dublin at Richmond Harbour in Clondra, where it meets the River Shannon.
Center Parcs Longford Forest, opened near Ballymahon in 2019, was one of the largest single tourism investments in the history of the Irish state.
The Norman motte at Granard is among the highest and best preserved in Ireland, marking the north-western limit of the early Anglo-Norman advance.

intro: They call it the Wee County, but Louth looms enormous in Irish myth. Ireland's smallest county is the setting for much of the Táin Bó Cúailnge, the great epic in which the boy-warrior Cú Chulainn single-handedly defended the Gap of the North against the armies of Queen Medb. The Cooley Peninsula, where the saga's famous brown bull grazed, is still one of the east coast's most dramatic landscapes, its mountains falling to Carlingford Lough. Even the county's name is mythic — it comes from the village of Louth, itself named for Lugh, the shining god of the Tuatha Dé Danann.

History kept returning to this narrow corridor between Dublin and Ulster. Mellifont, Ireland's first Cistercian abbey, rose here in 1142, and the high crosses of Monasterboice are among the finest carved stones of early Christian Europe. Drogheda endured Cromwell's most notorious siege and today guards the preserved head of St Oliver Plunkett; Dundalk grew into a proud industrial and brewing town. A border county with a strong GAA and soccer culture, modern Louth thrives along the M1 corridor, while Carlingford's medieval lanes and oyster festivals make it one of Ireland's most atmospheric small towns.

towns.name: Dundalk
towns.note: The county town, midway between Dublin and Belfast, an industrial and brewing centre long associated with Cú Chulainn, Harp Lager and Dundalk FC.

towns.name: Drogheda
towns.note: One of Ireland's largest towns, a historic walled port on the Boyne that holds the preserved head of St Oliver Plunkett in St Peter's Church.

towns.name: Ardee

towns.name: Carlingford

towns.name: Blackrock
towns.note: A seaside village on Dundalk Bay with a Victorian promenade, long a favourite bathing spot for the town.

towns.name: Clogherhead

towns.name: Termonfeckin

towns.name: Dunleer

towns.name: Omeath
towns.note: A village on Carlingford Lough that remained Irish-speaking into the early 20th century, the last Gaeltacht area in Leinster.

towns.name: Louth

facts: Louth is the smallest county in Ireland at roughly 826 square kilometres, earning it the nickname 'the Wee County'.
Mellifont Abbey, founded in 1142, was the first Cistercian monastery in Ireland and became the model for dozens of daughter houses across the country.
Muiredach's Cross at Monasterboice, standing about 5.5 metres tall, is widely considered the finest high cross in all of Ireland.
The preserved head of St Oliver Plunkett, executed at Tyburn in 1681 and canonised in 1975, is displayed in a shrine in St Peter's Church, Drogheda.
Louth is one of the only Irish counties named after a village — the tiny settlement of Louth, whose name derives from Lugh, the ancient Celtic god of light.
St Laurence's Gate in Drogheda is regarded as one of the finest surviving barbican gates in Europe, a relic of the town's medieval walls.
The capstone of the Proleek Dolmen near Dundalk weighs an estimated 35 tonnes and has balanced on its three supporting stones for some 5,000 years.
Omeath on the Cooley Peninsula was the last Irish-speaking district in Leinster, with native speakers surviving there into the 1920s.

intro: Meath's very name declares its status: An Mhí, the middle, heart of the ancient fifth province of Míde and seat of the High Kings of Ireland at Tara. This is the Royal County, and no county in Ireland is so saturated with the deep past. In the bend of the Boyne stand Newgrange, Knowth and Dowth — vast passage tombs raised around 3200 BC, older than Stonehenge or the pyramids of Giza, and together a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Each winter solstice, dawn light still creeps up the passage at Newgrange exactly as its builders intended more than five thousand years ago.

Later ages left their marks just as boldly. The monks of Kells produced one of the world's great manuscripts; Hugh de Lacy built Trim Castle, the largest Anglo-Norman fortress in Ireland; and in 1690 the fate of two kingdoms was decided at the Battle of the Boyne near Oldbridge. Meath's famously rich limestone pastures made it Ireland's great fattening ground for cattle, while Navan sits above Europe's largest zinc mine. Today it is a prosperous, fast-growing county in Dublin's orbit, fiercely proud of its Gaelic football tradition and of a heritage that few places on earth can match.

towns.name: Navan

towns.name: Athboy

towns.name: Ratoath

towns.name: Oldcastle

facts: Newgrange was built around 3200 BC, making it centuries older than Stonehenge and the Great Pyramid of Giza; its roof-box channels the winter solstice sunrise into the burial chamber.
The Hill of Tara was the ceremonial seat of the High Kings of Ireland, and its standing stone, the Lia Fáil, was said to cry out when touched by the rightful king.
Trim Castle took around 30 years to build from 1176 and is the largest Anglo-Norman castle in Ireland; it stood in for medieval York in the film Braveheart.
The Battle of the Boyne was fought near Oldbridge on 1 July 1690, when William III defeated James II in one of the most consequential battles in Irish history.
Tara Mines near Navan is the largest zinc mine in Europe, in production since 1977.
The Laytown Races, run since 1868, are the only official horse races in Europe held on a beach under the rules of racing.
Westmeath was part of Meath until 1543, when it was split off by act of parliament — both counties descend from the ancient kingdom of Míde, once counted as Ireland's fifth province.

The Tara Brooch, one of the greatest treasures of early Irish metalwork, was actually found on the beach at Bettystown in 1850 and has no connection to the Hill of Tara beyond its marketing-friendly name.
Halloween traces its roots to the festival of Samhain celebrated at Tlachtga, the Hill of Ward near Athboy, where great fires were lit to mark the Celtic new year.

intro: Few counties carry the weight of early Christian Ireland quite like Offaly. At Clonmacnoise, founded by St Ciaran around 544 where the Slighe Mhor road crossed the River Shannon, high kings of Ireland were buried among round towers and carved crosses, and the monastery grew into one of medieval Europe's great centres of learning. Shired in 1556 as King's County, in honour of Philip II of Spain during his marriage to Mary I, the county reclaimed its ancient name of Uibh Fhaili after independence. Its landscape is one of quiet drama: raised bogs, eskers left by retreating glaciers, and the rounded Slieve Bloom Mountains rising along the southern border.

For much of the twentieth century Offaly's economy ran on turf, with Bord na Mona harvesting the great midland bogs to feed power stations at Ferbane and Shannonbridge; today those same boglands are being rewetted and reimagined for wildlife and walking. Tullamore built a global whiskey brand, while Georgian Birr became an unlikely centre of Victorian science thanks to the astronomer earls of Rosse. Offaly people are famously understated, yet the county has punched far above its weight in sport, claiming All-Ireland titles in both hurling and football and producing an Open golf champion in Shane Lowry of Clara.

facts: Offaly was known as King's County from 1556 until independence, named for Philip II of Spain, then husband of Queen Mary I.
The Leviathan of Parsonstown at Birr Castle, completed in 1845, remained the largest telescope in the world for over seventy years.

In 1785 a crashed hot-air balloon set fire to Tullamore, destroying around 100 homes in what is often called the world's first aviation disaster; the town's crest features a phoenix rising from flames.
Old Croghan Man, an exceptionally tall Iron Age bog body over 2,000 years old, was discovered near Croghan Hill in 2003.
Seamus Darby's late goal for Offaly in the 1982 All-Ireland football final famously denied Kerry a historic five-in-a-row.
Tullamore D.E.W. whiskey takes its initials from Daniel E. Williams, the manager who built up the distillery in the late 1800s.
The box hedges in the gardens of Birr Castle are recognised as the tallest in the world.
Clonmacnoise was the burial place of the last High King of Ireland, Rory O'Connor, in 1198.

intro: Westmeath is Ireland's lake country, its low green hills threaded between Lough Ennell, Lough Owel, Lough Lene, Lough Derravaragh and the broad waters of Lough Ree on the Shannon. Myth runs deep here: the Children of Lir were said to have spent 300 years as swans on Derravaragh, and the Hill of Uisneach near Ballymore was regarded by the ancients as the sacred centre of Ireland, where the fires of Bealtaine were kindled and the provinces met at the great Catstone. Carved out of Meath by statute in 1543, the county has long been prosperous grazing land, celebrated for cattle so well fed the saying went 'beef to the heel like a Mullingar heifer'.

Its two principal towns pull in different directions: Mullingar, the county town, sits amid the lakes on the Royal Canal, while Athlone commands the Shannon crossing between Leinster and Connacht, its castle guarding a bridge fought over for centuries. Whiskey has been made at Kilbeggan since 1757, and music is a county tradition running from the tenor John McCormack through showband king Joe Dolan to Niall Horan of One Direction. With Goldsmith country along its western shore and Belvedere House on Lough Ennell, Westmeath rewards travellers who slow down and take to the water.

facts: Sean's Bar in Athlone is recognised by Guinness World Records as Ireland's oldest pub, with parts of the building dating to around 900 AD.
The Hill of Uisneach was regarded in early Ireland as the mystical centre of the island, and its Bealtaine fire festival has been revived in modern times.
In legend, the Children of Lir spent 300 of their 900 enchanted years as swans on Lough Derravaragh.
Westmeath was created in 1543 when an Act of Parliament divided the old county of Meath in two.
A townland on the shores of Lough Ennell is called Lilliput, a name local tradition links to Jonathan Swift, who visited the area before writing Gulliver's Travels.
From 1933 the high-power radio transmitter at Athlone broadcast to all of Europe, and 'Athlone' was marked on radio dials across the continent.
The Jealous Wall at Belvedere House, built by an earl to blot out his brother's home, is Ireland's largest folly.
Kilbeggan Distillery, licensed in 1757, is one of the oldest licensed whiskey distilleries in the world.

intro: History has a habit of arriving in Wexford by sea. The Vikings founded the county town as Waesfjord in the ninth century, and in 1169 the Normans made their first Irish landfall on the county's southern shore at Bannow Bay, changing the course of the island's story. In 1798 Wexford rose more fiercely than anywhere else in Ireland, and the pikemen of Boolavogue, the battle of Vinegar Hill and the short-lived Wexford Republic remain woven into the county's identity and its ballads. In the medieval baronies of Forth and Bargy, settlers' descendants spoke Yola, a unique dialect descended from Middle English, into the nineteenth century.

Known as the Model County for its progressive farming, Wexford enjoys more sunshine than most of Ireland, which is why its strawberries and early potatoes are famous nationwide. The fertile land rolls from the Blackstairs Mountains to long sandy beaches at Curracloe and Rosslare, where the Europort connects Ireland to Wales and France. Wexford town stages an internationally renowned opera festival each autumn, while New Ross tells the emigration story through the Dunbrody famine ship and the Kennedy Homestead at Dunganstown, the farm from which John F. Kennedy's great-grandfather set out in 1848.

facts: Hook Lighthouse on the Hook Peninsula has guided ships for some 800 years, making it one of the oldest operational lighthouses in the world.
Wexford takes its name from the Norse Waesfjord, meaning inlet of the mudflats.
Yola, a distinct language descended from Middle English, was spoken in the baronies of Forth and Bargy until the nineteenth century.
During the 1798 Rebellion, Wexford insurgents briefly declared an independent Wexford Republic before defeat at Vinegar Hill.
John F. Kennedy's great-grandfather Patrick emigrated from Dunganstown near New Ross in 1848, and JFK returned to the family farm as US president in June 1963.
Wexford Festival Opera, founded in 1951, built a global reputation by staging rare and forgotten operas.

The Normans made their first landing in Ireland in 1169 at Bannow Bay on the south Wexford coast.

intro: They call Wicklow the Garden of Ireland, but its beauty has a wild streak: the Wicklow Mountains form the largest continuous upland area in the country, a granite spine of heathery domes, glacial valleys and dark corrie lakes beginning barely an hour from Dublin city centre. In the valley of Glendalough, St Kevin founded a monastic settlement in the sixth century that grew into one of Ireland's most important religious sites, its round tower still standing between the two lakes. Those same mountains sheltered rebels for years after the 1798 Rising, prompting the British to cut the Military Road through the hills, today one of Ireland's most scenic drives.

Wicklow was the last of the traditional counties to be shired, in 1606, precisely because its terrain was so hard to subdue. Its later story is gentler: grand estates like Powerscourt and Parnell's Avondale, Victorian holidaymakers flocking to Bray on Brunel's railway, and a modern screen industry built around Ardmore Studios that has hosted everything from Braveheart to Vikings. Between the mountains and the sea runs a string of harbour and resort towns, while inland villages like Avoca and Enniskerry seem designed for postcards. For the diaspora, Wicklow offers Ireland in concentrate: monastic ruins, rebel history and mountain solitude within sight of the capital.

facts: Wicklow was the last of Ireland's traditional counties to be created, formally shired in 1606 because its mountains had resisted control for so long.
Lugnaquilla, at 925 metres, is the highest mountain in Ireland outside County Kerry.
Ireland's only gold rush took place in 1795 along the Goldmines River near Croghan Kinsella, where thousands panned for alluvial gold.
At 121 metres, Powerscourt Waterfall is generally cited as Ireland's highest year-round waterfall.
The railway around Bray Head, opened in the 1850s, was engineered by Isambard Kingdom Brunel.
The Military Road through the Wicklow Mountains was built by the British after 1798 to root out rebels such as Michael Dwyer hiding in the hills.
Lough Tay, the dark 'Guinness Lake' on the Luggala estate, doubled as Kattegat in the television series Vikings.
Wicklow has its own village called Hollywood, which displays a hillside sign echoing its Californian namesake.

intro: Few Irish counties pack in as much geological drama as Clare. The Burren, a vast limestone karst plateau in the north of the county, is a botanist's dream where arctic-alpine and Mediterranean plants grow side by side among grey stone pavements strewn with Neolithic tombs. To the south the land softens into farmland before ending abruptly at the Cliffs of Moher, which tower more than 200 metres above the Atlantic. Between them lie fishing villages, seaside resorts and the long finger of the Loop Head peninsula, while the county's eastern boundary is traced by Lough Derg and the River Shannon.

Clare is often called the home of Irish traditional music, and with reason: villages such as Doolin, Miltown Malbay and Feakle host sessions and summer schools that draw musicians from around the world. History runs deep too, from Brian Boru's power base at Killaloe to Michael Cusack of the Burren, who founded the GAA in 1884. The arrival of Shannon Airport in the 1940s transformed the county's economy, pioneering duty-free shopping and drawing industry to the mid-west. Known as the Banner County, Clare remains passionately devoted to hurling, and its 1995 All-Ireland win after an 81-year wait is the stuff of local legend.

towns.name: Ennis
towns.note: The county town, a medieval market town on the River Fergus known for its 13th-century Franciscan friary, narrow streets and lively traditional music scene.

towns.name: Kilrush
towns.note: A heritage town and marina port in west Clare, the gateway to Scattery Island's monastic ruins and dolphin-watching on the Shannon Estuary.

towns.name: Kilkee
towns.note: A Victorian seaside resort curved around a sheltered horseshoe bay, long a favourite bathing spot with dramatic cliff walks nearby.

towns.name: Doolin
towns.note: A coastal village famed worldwide as a hub of traditional music, and the departure point for ferries to the Aran Islands and Cliffs of Moher cruises.

towns.name: Lisdoonvarna
towns.note: A former Victorian spa town best known for its September Matchmaking Festival, one of Europe's largest singles gatherings.

towns.name: Ennistymon
towns.note: A characterful market town noted for its old painted shopfronts and the Cascades, where the River Inagh tumbles over rocky falls behind the main street.

towns.name: Killaloe
towns.note: A historic Lough Derg town linked by a 17-arch bridge to Ballina in Tipperary, and celebrated as the home place of High King Brian Boru.

towns.name: Miltown Malbay
towns.note: A west Clare town that hosts the Willie Clancy Summer School each July, Ireland's largest traditional music school.

towns.name: Bunratty
towns.note: A small village dominated by 15th-century Bunratty Castle and its folk park, one of Ireland's most visited heritage attractions.

towns.name: Corofin
towns.note: A village on the edge of the Burren that is home to the Clare Heritage Centre, a key stop for those tracing Clare ancestors.

people.name: Brian Boru
people.note: High King of Ireland who defeated the Vikings at Clontarf in 1014; his royal seat of Kincora was at Killaloe in east Clare.

people.name: Michael Cusack
people.note: Founder of the Gaelic Athletic Association in 1884, born in the Burren village of Carron where his cottage is now a visitor centre.

people.name: Edna O'Brien
people.note: Internationally acclaimed novelist, author of The Country Girls, born and raised in Tuamgraney in east Clare.

people.name: Willie Clancy
people.note: Master uilleann piper from Miltown Malbay whose legacy lives on in the summer school named in his honour.

people.name: Martin Hayes
people.note: One of the world's most celebrated traditional fiddlers, from Feakle, and a founding member of The Gloaming.

people.name: Sharon Shannon
people.note: Button accordion virtuoso from Ruan near Corofin, one of Ireland's best-known traditional musicians.

people.name: Keith Wood
people.note: Legendary Ireland and Lions rugby hooker, born in Killaloe, and the first-ever World Rugby Player of the Year in 2001.

people.name: Anthony Daly
people.note: Clarecastle hurler who captained Clare to their famous All-Ireland victories of 1995 and 1997.

people.name: Davy Fitzgerald
people.note: Sixmilebridge goalkeeper on Clare's 1995 and 1997 All-Ireland winning teams, later a high-profile intercounty manager.

people.name: Marty Morrissey
people.note: RTE's much-loved GAA commentator, raised in the seaside village of Quilty in west Clare.

facts: Shannon Airport opened the world's first duty-free shop in 1947, an idea that spread to airports across the globe.
The Poulnabrone dolmen in the Burren was built around 3800 BC, making it centuries older than the pyramids of Egypt.
Muhammad Ali's great-grandfather Abe Grady emigrated from Ennis in the 1860s, and the boxing legend visited the town to honour his roots in 2009.
Daniel O'Connell's victory in the 1828 Clare by-election forced the British government to grant Catholic Emancipation the following year.
The parochial house from the sitcom Father Ted stands near Kilnaboy, and much of the series was filmed around the Burren.
The Cliffs of Moher reach 214 metres at their highest point and attract well over a million visitors a year.
Clare is nicknamed the Banner County, a name linked to the banners carried at its great political rallies of the 19th century.
Spanish Point takes its name from ships of the Spanish Armada wrecked off the Clare coast in 1588.

intro: Ireland's largest county sprawls from rich dairy pasture in the north to the wild, fuchsia-hedged peninsulas of West Cork, where the land splinters into Mizen Head, Sheep's Head and Beara. At its heart sits Cork city, built on islands in the River Lee, a proudly independent merchant city whose people only half-jokingly call it the real capital. The county's coastline shaped its fortunes: Cork Harbour is one of the largest natural harbours in the world, and for generations Cobh was the last sight of Ireland for emigrants boarding ships for America, including passengers of the Titanic.

Cork earned its Rebel County nickname in the 15th century for backing the pretender Perkin Warbeck, and it lived up to the name during the War of Independence, when Michael Collins of Clonakilty led the fight and two of the city's Lord Mayors died for the cause. Today the county is as famous for food as for rebellion: the English Market has traded since 1788, Kinsale styles itself Ireland's gourmet capital, and Midleton distils some of the world's best-known whiskeys. Add a fierce hurling tradition, a thriving pharmaceutical and tech economy, and festivals from jazz to film, and Cork's confidence is easy to understand.

towns.name: Cork
towns.note: Ireland's second city, built on the River Lee, known for the English Market, Shandon's bells, University College Cork and a famously proud identity.

towns.name: Cobh
towns.note: The great emigration port on Cork Harbour, the Titanic's final port of call in 1912 and the departure point of Annie Moore, the first emigrant processed at Ellis Island.

towns.name: Kinsale
towns.note: A colourful harbour town regarded as Ireland's gourmet capital, and the site of the pivotal Battle of Kinsale in 1601.

towns.name: Clonakilty
towns.note: A lively West Cork town famous for its black pudding and as the heartland of Michael Collins, who was born nearby at Woodfield.

towns.name: Bantry
towns.note: A market town at the head of Bantry Bay, remembered for the failed French invasion fleet of 1796 and home to the elegant Bantry House.

towns.name: Skibbereen
towns.note: A West Cork town whose Famine story is among the most harrowing in Ireland, movingly told at its heritage centre.

towns.name: Youghal
towns.note: A walled medieval port at the mouth of the Blackwater once governed by Sir Walter Raleigh, and the filming location for the 1954 film Moby Dick.

towns.name: Midleton
towns.note: An east Cork town synonymous with whiskey, home to the distillery where Jameson and Midleton Very Rare are produced.

towns.name: Blarney
towns.note: A village just north of the city whose castle draws visitors from around the world to kiss the Blarney Stone for the gift of eloquence.

towns.name: Baltimore
towns.note: A sailing village in West Cork infamously sacked by Barbary pirates in 1631, now the gateway to Sherkin and Cape Clear islands.

people.name: Michael Collins
people.note: Revolutionary leader and Commander-in-Chief of the Free State army, born at Woodfield near Clonakilty in 1890.

people.name: Roy Keane
people.note: One of football's greatest midfielders and Manchester United's long-serving captain, from Mayfield in Cork city.

people.name: Sonia O'Sullivan
people.note: Olympic silver medallist and world champion runner from Cobh, one of Ireland's greatest ever athletes.

people.name: Cillian Murphy
people.note: Oscar-winning star of Oppenheimer and Peaky Blinders, born and raised in Cork city.

people.name: Rory Gallagher
people.note: Blues-rock guitar legend who grew up in Cork city, where a bronze statue and an annual festival honour him.

people.name: Jack Lynch
people.note: Twice Taoiseach and a Cork sporting icon who won six consecutive All-Ireland medals in hurling and football in the 1940s.

people.name: Mother Jones
people.note: Mary Harris Jones, the fearless American labour organiser once branded the most dangerous woman in America, was born in Cork city around 1837.

people.name: Christy Ring
people.note: Cloyne-born hurler widely regarded as one of the greatest players in the history of the game, winner of eight All-Ireland titles.

people.name: Terence MacSwiney
people.note: Lord Mayor of Cork whose 74-day hunger strike and death in 1920 drew worldwide attention to Ireland's independence struggle.

people.name: Graham Norton
people.note: The BBC's celebrated chat show host, who grew up in Bandon in West Cork.

facts: Cork is Ireland's largest county, and Cork Harbour is often described as one of the largest natural harbours in the world.
Annie Moore from Cork, the first immigrant ever processed at Ellis Island in 1892, sailed from Cobh, where her statue now stands on the quayside.
The Fastnet Rock off West Cork, Ireland's most southerly point, was nicknamed Ireland's Teardrop because it was the last piece of home emigrants saw.
Cork's English Market has been trading continuously since 1788 and was famously visited by Queen Elizabeth II in 2011.
The Rebel County nickname dates to 1491, when Cork backed Perkin Warbeck's claim to the English throne.
In 1631 pirates from the Barbary Coast sacked the village of Baltimore and carried off more than 100 inhabitants into slavery.
Henry Ford's father emigrated from Ballinascarthy near Clonakilty, and in 1917 Ford chose Cork city for its first purpose-built factory outside North America.
Cobh was called Queenstown when the Titanic made it her final port of call on 11 April 1912.

intro: They call it the Kingdom, and Kerry's subjects rarely argue. Ireland's most mountainous county contains the island's highest range, MacGillycuddy's Reeks, crowned by Carrauntoohil at 1,038 metres, and a coastline of peninsulas that reach far into the Atlantic. Off the Iveragh Peninsula rises Skellig Michael, where early Christian monks built beehive cells on a sea crag six centuries before the Normans came. The Dingle Peninsula shelters one of Ireland's strongest Gaeltacht communities, and the abandoned Blasket Islands produced an astonishing body of Irish-language literature from a tiny fishing population.

Tourism came early to Kerry: Victorian travellers flocked to Killarney's lakes, and the Muckross Estate later became the nucleus of Ireland's first national park in 1932. The county gave Ireland its greatest political figure of the 19th century in Daniel O'Connell of Derrynane, and its greatest Antarctic hero in Tom Crean of Annascaul. Listowel's literary tradition, led by John B. Keane, earned north Kerry a reputation as a writers' county, while in sport Kerry stands alone, having won more All-Ireland senior football titles than any other county. Emigration scattered Kerry people across the world, and the diaspora returns in great numbers every summer.

towns.name: Tralee
towns.note: The county town and commercial hub of Kerry, home of the Rose of Tralee festival held every August since 1959.

towns.name: Killarney
towns.note: Ireland's original tourist town, set beside the lakes, waterfalls and ancient oakwoods of Killarney National Park beneath MacGillycuddy's Reeks.

towns.name: Dingle
towns.note: A harbour town on its namesake peninsula famed for seafood, film links, its Gaeltacht hinterland and decades of association with Fungie the dolphin.

towns.name: Listowel
towns.note: North Kerry's literary capital, home town of playwright John B. Keane and host of Writers' Week, Ireland's oldest literary festival.

towns.name: Kenmare
towns.note: An elegant heritage town at the meeting point of the Ring of Kerry and the Beara Peninsula, noted for fine food and a Bronze Age stone circle.

towns.name: Cahersiveen
towns.note: The main town of the Iveragh Peninsula, birthplace area of Daniel O'Connell, whose memorial church is a rare one dedicated to a layman.

towns.name: Killorglin
towns.note: A town on the River Laune famous for Puck Fair, one of Ireland's oldest festivals, at which a wild mountain goat is crowned king each August.

towns.name: Waterville
towns.note: A Ring of Kerry seaside village beloved by Charlie Chaplin, who holidayed here for years and is remembered with a statue and film festival.

towns.name: Ballybunion
towns.note: A north Kerry resort renowned for its cliffs, beaches and a links golf course ranked among the finest in the world.

towns.name: Portmagee
towns.note: A fishing village connected by bridge to Valentia Island and the main departure point for boat trips to Skellig Michael.

people.name: Daniel O'Connell
people.note: The Liberator who won Catholic Emancipation in 1829, born near Cahersiveen and forever associated with his home at Derrynane.

people.name: Tom Crean
people.note: Antarctic explorer from Annascaul who served on three expeditions with Scott and Shackleton and later ran the South Pole Inn in his home village.

people.name: John B. Keane
people.note: Playwright and publican from Listowel whose works, including The Field and Sive, captured rural Irish life like few others.

people.name: St Brendan the Navigator
people.note: Sixth-century monk born near Tralee whose legendary Atlantic voyage made him the patron of sailors and a candidate for pre-Columbian discovery of America.

people.name: Peig Sayers
people.note: Storyteller of the Great Blasket Island whose autobiography became one of the most famous works of Irish-language literature.

people.name: Mick O'Dwyer
people.note: Waterville footballer and the most successful manager in Gaelic football history, guiding Kerry to eight All-Ireland titles.

people.name: Colm Cooper
people.note: Killarney's 'Gooch', regarded as one of the most skilful forwards ever to play Gaelic football.

people.name: Michael Fassbender
people.note: Hollywood star of films such as Hunger and 12 Years a Slave, raised in Killarney where his family ran a restaurant.

people.name: Brendan Kennelly

people.name: Jessie Buckley
people.note: Oscar-nominated actress and singer from Killarney, star of Wild Rose and Women Talking.

facts: Carrauntoohil in MacGillycuddy's Reeks is Ireland's highest mountain at 1,038 metres.
Skellig Michael, a UNESCO World Heritage Site with a 6th-century monastery, appeared as Luke Skywalker's refuge in the Star Wars films.
Valentia Island was the eastern terminus of the first permanently successful transatlantic telegraph cable, completed in 1866.
A fossilised tetrapod trackway on Valentia Island, roughly 385 million years old, records some of the earliest known footsteps of a four-legged creature on land.
Kerry has won more All-Ireland senior football championships than any other county, earning it the nickname the Kingdom of football.
Killarney National Park, created from the Muckross Estate in 1932, was Ireland's first national park.
The Great Blasket Island was finally abandoned in 1953, but its tiny community produced classic books by Peig Sayers, Tomas O Criomhthain and Muiris O Suilleabhain.
Charlie Chaplin holidayed in Waterville so often that the village now hosts an annual comedy film festival in his name.

intro: Founded by Vikings on an island in the Shannon in 922, Limerick city grew into one of Ireland's great medieval strongholds, its skyline still commanded by King John's Castle and St Mary's Cathedral. The city gave its name to the Treaty of Limerick of 1691, which ended the Williamite War and whose broken promises made Limerick the Treaty City. Beyond the city, the county spreads across the Golden Vale, some of the richest dairy farmland in Europe, dotted with medieval remnants at Kilmallock, Askeaton and Adare, whose thatched cottages make it one of Ireland's prettiest villages.

Limerick's modern story is one of reinvention. The Ardnacrusha hydroelectric scheme, completed on the Shannon in 1929, was a huge gamble by the young Free State that electrified the country. Frank McCourt's Angela's Ashes made the lanes of his childhood famous worldwide, while the city's passion for rugby, centred on Thomond Park and Munster's famous 1978 defeat of the All Blacks, is unmatched in Ireland. Recent decades brought a university, a thriving film industry and Limerick hurling's golden era, with the county dominating the game in the 2020s under John Kiely.

towns.name: Limerick
towns.note: The Treaty City on the Shannon, home to King John's Castle, the Hunt Museum, Thomond Park and Ireland's most fervent rugby tradition.

towns.name: Adare

towns.name: Kilmallock
towns.note: One of Ireland's best-preserved medieval walled towns, once a stronghold of the Earls of Desmond.

towns.name: Foynes
towns.note: A Shannon Estuary port that served as Europe's transatlantic flying boat terminal in the late 1930s and early 1940s, and the birthplace of Irish coffee.

towns.name: Askeaton

towns.name: Abbeyfeale

towns.name: Bruff

towns.name: Castleconnell

towns.name: Murroe
towns.note: An east Limerick village beside Glenstal Abbey, a Benedictine monastery and renowned boarding school.

people.name: Frank McCourt
people.note: Pulitzer Prize-winning author of Angela's Ashes, the memoir of his impoverished Limerick childhood.

people.name: Dolores O'Riordan

people.name: Terry Wogan

people.name: Kate O'Brien

facts: Irish coffee was invented at Foynes in the 1940s by chef Joe Sheridan to warm passengers from the transatlantic flying boats.
The Ardnacrusha hydroelectric scheme, completed in 1929, was among the largest in the world at the time and at first supplied most of the Free State's electricity.
Munster's 12-0 victory over the All Blacks at Thomond Park in 1978 remains one of rugby's most storied upsets, later celebrated in the play Alone It Stands.
Limerick city was founded by the Vikings in 922, making it one of Ireland's oldest cities.
The Treaty Stone on Clancy's Strand marks where the Treaty of Limerick was reputedly signed in 1691.
The five-line comic verse known as the limerick is named after the county, a link often traced to the refrain 'Will you come up to Limerick'.
Rose Fitzgerald Kennedy's ancestors, the maternal line of President John F. Kennedy, came from Bruff in south Limerick.
Adare Manor will host the Ryder Cup in 2027, bringing the contest to Limerick for the first time.

intro: Ireland's largest inland county sprawls across the heart of Munster, its name known around the world thanks to a marching song written by a man who likely never set foot in it. Tipperary's wealth has always come from its land: the Golden Vale, some of the richest dairy pasture in Europe, rolls between the Galtee, Knockmealdown and Silvermine mountains, and the River Suir threads the county from its source near Templemore down through Thurles, Cahir and Clonmel. That fertility drew Norman castles and great abbeys, and later made the county a stronghold of prosperous farming, horse breeding and agitation over land rights alike.

History sits heavily and proudly here. The Rock of Cashel, seat of the Kings of Munster before it passed to the church in 1101, is one of Ireland's most spectacular monuments, while the Gaelic Athletic Association was founded in a Thurles hotel in 1884, making the county a cradle of hurling ever since. The War of Independence effectively began at Soloheadbeg in 1919, and Fenian tradition runs deep through figures like Kickham and O'Leary. Until 2014 Tipperary was unique in being split into two administrative ridings, North and South, each with its own county town.

towns.name: Clonmel
towns.note: The county's largest town, on the Suir beneath the Comeraghs, long famous for Bulmers cider and as the birthplace of novelist Laurence Sterne.

towns.name: Nenagh
towns.note: Former county town of North Tipperary, dominated by a superb 13th-century Norman castle keep and now a thriving food and market town.

towns.name: Thurles
towns.note: Cathedral town where the GAA was founded at Hayes' Hotel in 1884, and home to Semple Stadium, hurling's most storied provincial ground.

towns.name: Cashel
towns.note: Heritage town at the foot of the Rock of Cashel, whose round tower, Cormac's Chapel and ruined cathedral crown an ancient royal site.

towns.name: Tipperary Town
towns.note: The market town that gave the county its name, set in the Golden Vale with a strong Fenian and land-agitation history.

towns.name: Cahir
towns.note: Home to one of Ireland's largest and best-preserved castles on an island in the Suir, plus the ornamental Swiss Cottage nearby.

towns.name: Carrick-on-Suir
towns.note: Riverside town holding Ormond Castle, Ireland's finest Tudor manor house, and proudly linked to cycling great Sean Kelly.

towns.name: Roscrea
towns.note: One of Ireland's oldest towns, grown around a 7th-century monastery, with a round tower, high cross and Damer House castle complex.

towns.name: Templemore
towns.note: Trim north-county town best known as the home of the Garda Siochana training college.

towns.name: Fethard
towns.note: Small medieval town with the most complete circuit of town walls surviving in Ireland, close to the Coolmore horse-breeding empire.

people.name: Charles Kickham
people.note: Mullinahone-born Fenian leader and author of Knocknagow, one of the most widely read Irish novels of the 19th century.

people.name: Laurence Sterne
people.note: Author of Tristram Shandy, one of the great experimental novels in English, born in Clonmel in 1713.

people.name: John O'Leary
people.note: Tipperary Town-born Fenian intellectual immortalised in Yeats's line that romantic Ireland was dead and gone, with O'Leary in the grave.

people.name: Dan Breen
people.note: Soloheadbeg-born IRA leader whose 1919 ambush is regarded as the opening action of the War of Independence.

people.name: Sean Treacy
people.note: Republican from near Tipperary Town who led the Soloheadbeg ambush alongside Breen and died in a Dublin gunfight in 1920.

people.name: Sean Kelly
people.note: One of cycling's all-time greats, winner of Paris-Roubaix and the Vuelta, raised on a farm outside Carrick-on-Suir.

people.name: Frank Patterson
people.note: Clonmel-born tenor known as Ireland's Golden Voice, who sang for popes, presidents and in The Dead and Miller's Crossing.

people.name: Pat Shortt
people.note: Thurles-born comedian and actor, half of D'Unbelievables and award-winning star of the film Garage.

people.name: Una Healy
