people.name: Shane Long
people.note: Republic of Ireland striker from Gortnahoe who scored the fastest goal in Premier League history in 2019.

facts: The Gaelic Athletic Association was founded in the billiard room of Hayes' Hotel, Thurles, on 1 November 1884.
Until 2014 Tipperary was the only Irish county divided into two separate ridings, North and South, each with its own county council.
Galtymore, at around 917 metres, is the highest inland mountain in Ireland.
The Soloheadbeg ambush of 21 January 1919, seen as the first action of the War of Independence, took place on the same day the First Dail met in Dublin.
It's a Long Way to Tipperary, the great marching song of the First World War, was written in 1912 by Jack Judge, an Englishman of Irish descent.
Coolmore Stud near Fethard is the largest thoroughbred racehorse breeding operation in the world.
The Hogan Stand at Croke Park is named after Michael Hogan of Grangemockler, the Tipperary footballer shot dead on Bloody Sunday in 1920.
Tipperary is the largest of Ireland's inland counties, and the Rock of Cashel was reputedly handed to the church in 1101 by King Muirchertach Ua Briain.

intro: No Irish city is older than Waterford. Viking raiders founded Vadrarfjordr in 914, and the city's Reginald's Tower, medieval walls and Viking Triangle museums still tell the story of a port that Norman, Tudor and Georgian rulers all prized. Strongbow married Aoife here in 1170, sealing the Norman entry into Ireland, and in 1848 Thomas Francis Meagher first flew the Irish tricolour from a window on the Mall. The county's name became a global byword for elegance through Waterford Crystal, founded by the Penrose brothers in 1783 and still cut in the city today.

Beyond the city, the Deise, as locals call the county, packs remarkable variety into a small space: the Copper Coast's cliffs and coves form a UNESCO Global Geopark, the Comeragh Mountains hold glacial corrie lakes like Coumshingaun, and the Blackwater valley around Lismore is lush castle country. An Rinn, near Dungarvan, keeps a living Gaeltacht alive in the sunny south-east, while the 46-kilometre Waterford Greenway along an old railway has become one of Ireland's favourite cycling routes. The local blaa, a soft white bread roll, is so distinctive it holds protected European status.

towns.name: Waterford City
towns.note: Ireland's oldest city, founded by Vikings in 914, home to Reginald's Tower, the Viking Triangle museums and the House of Waterford Crystal.

towns.name: Dungarvan
towns.note: Harbour town beneath the Comeraghs that anchors the Waterford Greenway and has grown into a celebrated food destination.

towns.name: Tramore
towns.note: Classic seaside resort with a five-kilometre strand, a promenade, surf schools and one of Ireland's best-loved racecourses.

towns.name: Lismore
towns.note: Heritage town on the Blackwater dominated by Lismore Castle, Irish seat of the Dukes of Devonshire and birthplace of scientist Robert Boyle.

towns.name: An Rinn
towns.note: Heart of Gaeltacht na nDeise, where Irish remains a community language and students flock to summer colleges.

towns.name: Ardmore
towns.note: Cliff-walk village where St Declan founded a Christian settlement said to predate St Patrick, marked by a slender 12th-century round tower.

towns.name: Portlaw
towns.note: Planned model village built by the Quaker Malcomson family around their 19th-century cotton mill.

towns.name: Kilmacthomas
towns.note: Comeragh-foothills village whose great stone viaduct is now a highlight of the Waterford Greenway.

towns.name: Passage East
towns.note: Fishing village where a car ferry crosses the estuary to Wexford, near the spot where the Normans landed in force.

people.name: Robert Boyle
people.note: The father of modern chemistry and author of Boyle's Law, born at Lismore Castle in 1627.

people.name: Ernest Walton
people.note: Physicist born in Abbeyside, Dungarvan, who split the atomic nucleus with Cockcroft and won the 1951 Nobel Prize, Ireland's only science Nobel.

people.name: Thomas Francis Meagher
people.note: Waterford-born Young Irelander who first flew the tricolour in his native city in 1848 and later became a Union general and governor of Montana.

people.name: Luke Wadding
people.note: Waterford-born Franciscan scholar credited with having St Patrick's Day placed on the church's universal calendar.

people.name: John Roberts
people.note: 18th-century Waterford architect with the rare distinction of designing both the city's Protestant and Catholic cathedrals.

people.name: Val Doonican
people.note: Waterford city crooner whose easy-going BBC television show made him a household name across Britain and Ireland for decades.

people.name: Gilbert O'Sullivan
people.note: Singer-songwriter of Alone Again (Naturally) and Clair, born Raymond O'Sullivan in Waterford in 1946.

people.name: Anna Manahan
people.note: Waterford actress who won a Tony Award for The Beauty Queen of Leenane after a long career on Irish stages.

people.name: John Treacy
people.note: Villierstown athlete who won two World Cross Country titles and marathon silver at the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics.

people.name: Tyrone Power
people.note: The celebrated 19th-century Irish comic actor, founder of the Hollywood acting dynasty, born near Kilmacthomas in 1795.

facts: Waterford is Ireland's oldest city, founded by Vikings in 914, several decades before Dublin received its city charter.
The Irish tricolour was first flown in public by Thomas Francis Meagher at 33 The Mall, Waterford, on 7 March 1848.
Jacob's, the bakery firm that went on to invent the cream cracker, was founded in Waterford in 1851 before moving to Dublin.
The Waterford blaa, a soft floury bread roll of Huguenot origin, was granted EU Protected Geographical Indication status in 2013.
The marriage of Strongbow and Aoife, which bound Ireland to the Norman world, took place in Waterford in 1170.
The Copper Coast between Tramore and Dungarvan is a UNESCO Global Geopark named for its 19th-century copper mines.
Waterford Crystal was founded by brothers George and William Penrose in 1783.
Ardmore claims to be Ireland's oldest Christian settlement, founded by St Declan before St Patrick's mission began.

intro: Few counties divide so dramatically in two. East of Lough Corrib, the Republic's largest lake, Galway is limestone farmland dotted with market towns, castles and monastic ruins; west of it lies Connemara, a wild sweep of blanket bog, quartzite peaks and Atlantic inlets where Ireland's largest Gaeltacht keeps the Irish language in daily use. The Aran Islands guard the mouth of the bay, their limestone pavements and stone forts, including the great cliff fortress of Dun Aonghasa, linking the county to millennia of settlement. The Connemara pony, Ireland's only native pony breed, still grazes the hillsides that shaped it.

Galway city grew rich on medieval trade with Spain and France under the fourteen merchant families known as the Tribes, and it wears that history lightly amid a famously bohemian street life of buskers, festivals and theatre, led by the Druid company and the summer Arts Festival. The Claddagh ring, with its heart, hands and crown, originated in the old fishing village across the Corrib. Race week at Ballybrit, the September oyster festival and the horse fair at Ballinasloe fill the calendar, and in 2020 the city held the title of European Capital of Culture.

towns.name: Galway City
towns.note: The fast-growing City of the Tribes, a university city famed for its festivals, medieval Latin Quarter and position where the Corrib meets the Atlantic.

towns.name: Clifden
towns.note: Connemara's capital, founded in 1812, close to where Alcock and Brown ended the first nonstop transatlantic flight and Marconi built his wireless station.

towns.name: Tuam
towns.note: Ancient ecclesiastical centre of the west, seat of archbishops since the 12th century and once the power base of the O'Connor high kings.

towns.name: An Spideal
towns.note: Gateway village to the Cois Fharraige Gaeltacht, known for its craft village, summer colleges and strong traditional music scene.

towns.name: Athenry
towns.note: One of Ireland's best-preserved medieval walled towns, with castle, priory and the name known worldwide from the ballad The Fields of Athenry.

towns.name: Ballinasloe
towns.note: Market town on the Suck whose October horse fair is among the oldest and largest in Europe.

towns.name: Loughrea
towns.note: Lakeside town whose cathedral holds an outstanding collection of Irish Arts and Crafts stained glass.

towns.name: Oughterard
towns.note: Angling village on the shore of Lough Corrib, long styled the gateway to Connemara.

towns.name: Portumna
towns.note: Shannonside heritage town with a great semi-fortified Jacobean house and forest park where Lough Derg begins.

towns.name: Kinvara
towns.note: Picturesque harbour village on Galway Bay beside Dunguaire Castle, host of the Cruinniu na mBad gathering of traditional sailing boats.

people.name: Lady Augusta Gregory
people.note: Playwright and co-founder of the Abbey Theatre whose home at Coole Park near Gort was the hub of the Irish Literary Revival.

people.name: Nora Barnacle
people.note: Galway city woman who became James Joyce's muse and wife; their first walk together on 16 June 1904 is commemorated as Bloomsday.

people.name: Padraic O Conaire
people.note: Pioneering Irish-language writer and wandering storyteller from Galway city, honoured with a famous statue in Eyre Square.

people.name: Mairtin O Cadhain
people.note: Author of Cre na Cille, widely considered the greatest Irish-language novel, born in the Cois Fharraige Gaeltacht near An Spideal.

people.name: Walter Macken
people.note: Galway city novelist, playwright and actor best remembered for the historical trilogy beginning with Seek the Fair Land.

people.name: Richard Kirwan
people.note: Eccentric 18th-century chemist and mineralogist from Cloughballymore, one of the most celebrated Irish scientists of his day.

people.name: Michael D. Higgins
people.note: President of Ireland since 2011, long a Galway West TD, university lecturer and Mayor of Galway before entering national politics.

people.name: Nicola Coughlan
people.note: Galway-born actress who found global fame in Derry Girls and Bridgerton.

people.name: Joe Canning
people.note: Portumna hurler regarded as one of the greatest forwards ever, Hurler of the Year when Galway won the 2017 All-Ireland.

people.name: Dolores Keane
people.note: Caherlistrane-born singer, founding member of De Dannan and one of the defining voices of Irish traditional song.

facts: Alcock and Brown completed the first nonstop transatlantic flight by crash-landing in Derrygimlagh bog near Clifden on 15 June 1919.
Marconi opened his first permanent transatlantic wireless telegraphy station at Clifden in 1907, employing hundreds in remote Connemara.
Lough Corrib is the largest lake in the Republic of Ireland and second largest on the island after Lough Neagh.
The Galway International Oyster Festival, founded in 1954, is billed as the oldest oyster festival in the world.
The Connemara pony is Ireland's only native breed of pony, shaped by the region's rough terrain.
The Claddagh ring takes its name from the old fishing village of the Claddagh, just across the Corrib from Galway city's Spanish Arch.
Galway city takes its nickname from the fourteen merchant Tribes, families such as the Lynches and Blakes who ran the town for centuries.
The Benedictine nuns of Kylemore Abbey settled in Connemara in 1920 after their community fled Ypres during the First World War.

intro: Quietly beautiful and often overlooked, Leitrim is Ireland's least populous county, a place of drumlins, rushy fields and an extraordinary amount of water: Lough Allen splits it almost in two, the Shannon rises just beyond its border and glides through it, and dozens of smaller lakes stock some of the best coarse fishing in Europe. Sliabh an Iarainn, the Iron Mountain, recalls centuries of iron working above Lough Allen. The Famine hit Leitrim harder than almost anywhere; a county of more than 150,000 people in 1841 fell decade after decade, and its story is written in emigrant letters across America, Britain and Australia.

That history of leaving gives Leitrim a special pull for the diaspora, and the county has quietly reinvented itself around its waterways, artists and food producers. The reopening of the Ballinamore-Ballyconnell canal as the Shannon-Erne Waterway in 1994 turned Carrick-on-Shannon into one of Ireland's busiest boating towns, while Drumshanbo's gin has carried the county's name around the world. This was O'Rourke country, the kingdom of Breifne ruled from Dromahair, and it later gave the 1916 Rising one of its signatories, Sean Mac Diarmada, whose thatched birthplace still stands at Kiltyclogher.

towns.name: Carrick-on-Shannon
towns.note: The lively county town and cruiser capital of the Shannon, home to the tiny Costello Memorial Chapel, the smallest in Ireland.

towns.name: Manorhamilton
towns.note: Chief town of scenic north Leitrim, grown around the ruined 1630s castle of Sir Frederick Hamilton amid glacial valleys.

towns.name: Drumshanbo
towns.note: Town at the foot of Sliabh an Iarainn famed for the Joe Mooney Summer School of traditional music and as the home of Gunpowder Irish Gin.

towns.name: Mohill
towns.note: Market town closely associated with the blind harper Turlough O'Carolan, who is commemorated with a statue in its main street.

towns.name: Ballinamore
towns.note: Friendly canal town on the Shannon-Erne Waterway with a strong angling and genealogy-research tradition.

towns.name: Dromahair
towns.note: Village on the Bonet that was the seat of the O'Rourkes of Breifne, near the ruins of Creevelea Friary and Parke's Castle on Lough Gill.

towns.name: Kiltyclogher
towns.note: Border village where 1916 leader Sean Mac Diarmada was born; his thatched homestead is preserved as a national monument.

towns.name: Drumsna
towns.note: Shannonside village where Anthony Trollope, working for the postal service, found the inspiration for his first novel.

towns.name: Kinlough
towns.note: Village near Lough Melvin, a lake renowned among anglers for trout varieties found almost nowhere else.

towns.name: Tullaghan
towns.note: Leitrim's only coastal village, standing on the county's tiny sliver of Atlantic shoreline.

people.name: Sean Mac Diarmada
people.note: Signatory of the 1916 Proclamation and chief organiser of the Rising, born at Corranmore near Kiltyclogher in 1883.

people.name: John McGahern
people.note: One of the finest Irish novelists of the 20th century, raised in and around Aughawillan and later farming near Fenagh, where books like Amongst Women are set.

people.name: Margaret Haughery
people.note: The Bread Woman of New Orleans, a famine-era emigrant from Carrigallen whose charity made her one of the first women honoured with a public statue in America.

people.name: Thomas Heazle Parke
people.note: Surgeon and explorer from Drumsna, the first Irishman to cross Africa, whose statue stands outside the Natural History Museum in Dublin.

people.name: Turlough O'Carolan
people.note: The great blind harper and composer spent much of his life around Mohill, which honours him with a bronze statue.

people.name: Brian O'Rourke
people.note: Lord of West Breifne who sheltered survivors of the Spanish Armada and was executed at Tyburn in 1591 for his defiance of the Crown.

people.name: Packie McGarty
people.note: Mohill-born Gaelic footballer of the 1950s and 60s, widely regarded as the greatest player never to win a major national honour.

people.name: Charlie McGettigan
people.note: Singer-songwriter long based in Drumshanbo who won the 1994 Eurovision Song Contest with Rock 'n' Roll Kids.

facts: Leitrim has the shortest coastline of any coastal county in Ireland, roughly four kilometres of Atlantic shore at Tullaghan.
It is the least populous county in Ireland, having fallen from over 150,000 people before the Famine.
The Costello Memorial Chapel in Carrick-on-Shannon, built in 1879 by a grieving husband, is the smallest chapel in Ireland and one of the smallest in the world.
The Shannon-Erne Waterway, reopened in 1994 along the old Ballinamore-Ballyconnell canal, reconnected Ireland's two great river systems through Leitrim.
Lough Melvin holds the gillaroo and sonaghan, genetically distinct trout found in very few waters anywhere in the world.
Anthony Trollope began his first novel, The Macdermots of Ballycloran, after being struck by a ruined house he saw while stationed at Drumsna.
Glencar Waterfall, on the Leitrim side of Glencar Lough, features in W. B. Yeats's poem The Stolen Child.
Leitrim's 1994 Connacht senior football title was only its second ever, the first having come in 1927.

intro: Few counties carry the weight of Irish history quite like Mayo. Its name comes from Maigh Eo, the plain of the yew trees, but its story is written in stone and bog: the Céide Fields on the north coast preserve the most extensive Stone Age field system known anywhere in the world, farmed some 6,000 years ago and then sealed beneath blanket bog. Later centuries were harder. Mayo was among the counties most devastated by the Great Famine, and mass emigration scattered its people from Cleveland to Coventry, which is why so many of the diaspora trace a line back to parishes around Ballina, Westport and Erris.

The landscape is the wildest in Connacht: the fjord of Killary Harbour on the Galway border, the sheer sea cliffs of Achill, the vast empty boglands of Erris, and the holy mountain of Croagh Patrick rising above Clew Bay and its scatter of drumlin islands. The county was the crucible of the Land War, launched from Irishtown in 1879, and the word boycott itself was coined here, after Lough Mask land agent Captain Charles Boycott. Today tourism, agriculture and a cluster of pharmaceutical employers around Castlebar and Westport anchor the economy, while Mayo GAA supporters remain famous for hope in the face of heartbreak.

towns.name: Castlebar
towns.note: The county town and administrative heart of Mayo, remembered for the Races of Castlebar in 1798, when French and Irish forces routed a British garrison.

towns.name: Westport
towns.note: A rare planned Georgian town laid out in the 1780s, sitting at the foot of Croagh Patrick and repeatedly voted among the best places to live in Ireland.

towns.name: Ballina
towns.note: North Mayo's biggest town, world-famous for salmon fishing on the River Moy and the home place of President Mary Robinson.

towns.name: Knock
towns.note: Village transformed by the 1879 apparition witnessed by fifteen local people, now an international Marian shrine visited by around a million pilgrims a year.

towns.name: Keel (Achill)
towns.note: Achill Island's main village, strung along a sweeping three-kilometre beach beneath the Minaun Cliffs.

towns.name: Dooagh (Achill)
towns.note: Achill village near Keem Bay where ocean rower Don Allum came ashore in 1987, and whose vanished beach famously reappeared overnight in 2017.

towns.name: Belmullet
towns.note: The market town of remote Erris, gateway to the Mullet Peninsula, the Irish-speaking Gaeltacht and some of Europe's darkest night skies.

towns.name: Cong
towns.note: Picture-postcard village on the Galway border where John Ford filmed The Quiet Man in 1951, beside the five-star Ashford Castle estate.

towns.name: Foxford
towns.note: Moy-side town known for its woollen mills, founded in 1892 and still weaving, and as the birthplace of Admiral William Brown.

towns.name: Claremorris
towns.note: Busy rail-junction town in south Mayo that grew as a market and transport hub for the surrounding plains.

people.name: Mary Robinson
people.note: Ballina-born barrister who became Ireland's first female President in 1990 and later UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.

people.name: Grace O'Malley (Gráinne Mhaol)
people.note: The 16th-century pirate queen of Clew Bay who commanded her own fleet and famously met Elizabeth I face to face in 1593.

people.name: Michael Davitt
people.note: Founder of the Land League, born in Straide in 1846 and evicted with his family as a child, an experience that shaped the Land War he led.

people.name: Admiral William Brown
people.note: Foxford emigrant who founded the Argentine Navy and is honoured as a national hero of Argentina, with over a thousand streets there bearing his name.

people.name: Martin Sheridan
people.note: Bohola-born athlete who won five Olympic gold medals for the United States in the early 1900s as one of the famed Irish Whales.

people.name: Margaret Burke Sheridan
people.note: Castlebar-born soprano who became one of the great Madama Butterfly interpreters at La Scala and was dubbed the Empress of Ireland by Toscanini's Milan.

people.name: John MacBride
people.note: Westport-born republican, executed after the 1916 Rising, husband of Maud Gonne and father of Nobel laureate Seán MacBride.

people.name: Enda Kenny
people.note: Castlebar politician who served as Taoiseach from 2011 to 2017, the longest-serving Fine Gael leader in the office.

people.name: Louis Walsh
people.note: Kiltimagh-born music manager behind Boyzone and Westlife and a long-running judge on The X Factor.

people.name: Sally Rooney
people.note: Castlebar-raised novelist whose books Normal People and Conversations with Friends made her one of the most acclaimed writers of her generation.

facts: The Céide Fields near Ballycastle are the most extensive Stone Age field system in the world, walled farmland roughly 6,000 years old preserved under blanket bog.
Achill is Ireland's largest offshore island, joined to the mainland by a bridge since 1887.
Mayo footballers have not won the All-Ireland senior title since 1951 despite reaching numerous finals, giving rise to the famous legend of the 'curse of 51'.
Ireland West Airport Knock opened in 1985 on a foggy boggy hilltop after a campaign by local parish priest Monsignor James Horan, and now handles hundreds of thousands of passengers a year.
On Reek Sunday, the last Sunday of July, thousands of pilgrims climb Croagh Patrick, some barefoot, continuing a pilgrimage tradition well over a thousand years old.
The word boycott entered the English language in Mayo in 1880, when the community around Lough Mask ostracised land agent Captain Charles Boycott.
The Great Western Greenway, running 42 kilometres from Westport to Achill along a disused railway, was Ireland's first great off-road greenway when it fully opened in 2011.
In 1987 Don Allum landed at Dooagh on Achill to become the first person to row the Atlantic in both directions.

intro: Roscommon is royal country. At Rathcroghan near Tulsk lies Cruachan, the ancient capital of Connacht and seat of the legendary Queen Medb, a complex of more than 240 archaeological sites spread across the plains. The O'Conor kings of Connacht ruled from here, and two of them, Turlough and Rory, were the last High Kings of Ireland; remarkably, their descendants still live at Clonalis House in Castlerea, one of the oldest documented family lines in Europe. The county's name comes from Ros Comáin, the wood of St Comán, who founded a monastery where the county town now stands.

This is a quiet, low-lying county of cattle pasture, esker ridges and water, bounded by the Shannon to the east and the River Suck to the west, and the only county in Connacht without a coastline. It bore a terrible share of Famine suffering, losing a greater proportion of its population than almost any other county, a history confronted head-on at the National Famine Museum in Strokestown. Sheep and suckler farming still shape rural life, Lough Key Forest Park draws visitors to the north, and the county's scattered diaspora keeps strong ties to towns like Boyle, Elphin and Ballaghaderreen.

towns.name: Roscommon
towns.note: The county town, dominated by the ruins of its 13th-century Anglo-Norman castle and a Dominican priory founded in 1253.

towns.name: Boyle
towns.note: Handsome north Roscommon town beside Lough Key, home to the beautifully preserved 12th-century Cistercian Boyle Abbey and the Georgian King House.

towns.name: Castlerea
towns.note: Market town on the River Suck beside Clonalis House, ancestral home of the O'Conors, descendants of the last High Kings of Ireland.

towns.name: Strokestown
towns.note: Planned estate town whose Palladian big house now holds the National Famine Museum, documenting the 1847 emigration of 1,490 tenants.

towns.name: Elphin
towns.note: One of Ireland's oldest ecclesiastical centres, a diocese traditionally founded by St Patrick, with a restored 18th-century windmill.

towns.name: Ballaghaderreen
towns.note: West Roscommon market town with a cathedral, transferred from County Mayo to Roscommon by boundary changes in 1898.

towns.name: Frenchpark
towns.note: Village where Douglas Hyde, founder of the Gaelic League and first President of Ireland, grew up in the local rectory.

towns.name: Tulsk
towns.note: Small village at the heart of the Rathcroghan complex, ancient royal site of Connacht, with a visitor centre interpreting Queen Medb's Cruachan.

people.name: Douglas Hyde
people.note: First President of Ireland and founder of the Gaelic League, raised at Frenchpark where his father was Church of Ireland rector.

people.name: Rory O'Conor (Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair)
people.note: King of Connacht and the last High King of Ireland, whose reign ended with the Anglo-Norman invasion of the 12th century.

people.name: Turlough O'Carolan
people.note: The celebrated blind harper and composer spent much of his life under Roscommon patronage and is buried at Kilronan near Ballyfarnon.

people.name: Percy French
people.note: One of Ireland's best-loved songwriters, composer of The Mountains of Mourne, born at Cloonyquin House near Tulsk in 1854.

people.name: Maureen O'Sullivan
people.note: Boyle-born Hollywood star who played Jane in the Tarzan films of the 1930s and was mother of actress Mia Farrow.

people.name: Chris O'Dowd
people.note: Boyle-born actor and comedian of Bridesmaids and The IT Crowd fame, who set his Sky series Moone Boy in his hometown.

people.name: Albert Reynolds
people.note: Taoiseach from 1992 to 1994 and a key architect of the Northern Ireland peace process, born in Rooskey on the Roscommon-Leitrim border.

people.name: Sir William Wilde
people.note: Eminent Victorian eye surgeon, antiquarian and father of Oscar Wilde, born near Castlerea in 1815.

facts: Roscommon is the only landlocked county in Connacht, bounded instead by the River Shannon and the River Suck.
The cave of Oweynagat at Rathcroghan was described in medieval literature as Ireland's gate to hell, and folklorists link the site to the origins of Samhain, the festival behind Halloween.
According to well-documented local history, an 18th-century condemned prisoner known as Lady Betty was spared execution at Roscommon jail on condition she serve as the town's hangwoman.
Coal was mined at Arigna in north Roscommon for around 400 years until 1990, when Ireland's last working coal mine closed; it is now a visitor experience.
Clonalis House in Castlerea, home of the O'Conor family, preserves the harp of the composer Turlough O'Carolan among its heirlooms.
The main street of Strokestown was reputedly laid out to be one of the widest in Ireland, inspired by the grand boulevards of Vienna.
The National Famine Way, a 165-kilometre walking trail, follows the 1847 route of 1,490 evicted Strokestown tenants who walked to the Dublin ships.
Douglas Hyde of Frenchpark became the first President of Ireland in 1938, having earlier founded the Gaelic League to revive the Irish language.

intro: Yeats called it the Land of Heart's Desire, and Sligo's landscape explains why: the great flat-topped prow of Benbulben, the cairn-crowned summit of Knocknarea, Lough Gill with its Isle of Innisfree, and Atlantic strands running from Enniscrone to Mullaghmore. W.B. Yeats spent his childhood summers here with his Pollexfen relations and asked to be buried at Drumcliff in Benbulben's shadow, while his brother Jack painted the county's horses, fairs and shorelines. But Sligo's story is far older than the Yeatses: the megalithic cemetery at Carrowmore is among the largest and most ancient in Ireland.

The name comes from Sligeach, the shelly place, after the abundant shellfish of the Garavogue estuary, and the sea still defines the county. Strandhill and Easkey are internationally known surfing breaks, Mullaghmore draws big-wave riders from around the world, and the Edwardian seaweed baths of Enniscrone carry on a distinctly Sligo cure. The town itself is the commercial capital of the north-west, with a strong traditional music heritage in the south of the county around Tubbercurry and Gurteen, the homeland of fiddle legend Michael Coleman, whose American recordings shaped Irish music worldwide.

towns.name: Sligo
towns.note: The county town and largest urban centre in the north-west, straddling the Garavogue river, rich in Yeats associations and home to a 13th-century abbey.

towns.name: Strandhill
towns.note: Surfing village beneath Knocknarea with a famous beach break, seaweed baths and a seafront where swimming is banned but surfing thrives.

towns.name: Rosses Point
towns.note: Seaside village loved by the Yeats brothers, with a championship links course and the Metal Man beacon guiding ships since 1821.

towns.name: Enniscrone
towns.note: West Sligo resort on Killala Bay known for its five-kilometre beach and Kilcullen's hot seaweed baths, in business since 1912.

towns.name: Tubbercurry
towns.note: South Sligo's largest town and a stronghold of traditional music, hosting the South Sligo Summer School each July.

towns.name: Ballymote
towns.note: Market town with a great Norman castle where the Book of Ballymote, key to deciphering ogham script, was compiled around 1391.

towns.name: Drumcliff
towns.note: Village beneath Benbulben where W.B. Yeats is buried in the churchyard of a monastery founded by St Colmcille, under his own epitaph.

towns.name: Mullaghmore
towns.note: Harbour village with a big-wave surf reef offshore, overlooked by Classiebawn Castle, the summer home of Lord Mountbatten.

towns.name: Grange
towns.note: North Sligo village near Streedagh Strand, where three ships of the Spanish Armada were wrecked in 1588.

people.name: W.B. Yeats
people.note: Nobel Prize-winning poet who spent formative childhood summers in Sligo, drew lifelong inspiration from its landscape, and is buried at Drumcliff.

people.name: Jack B. Yeats
people.note: Ireland's most celebrated 20th-century painter, raised in Sligo with his grandparents, whose scenes of west of Ireland life won Ireland's first Olympic medal, for art, in 1924.

people.name: Constance Markievicz
people.note: 1916 Rising leader and the first woman elected to the Westminster parliament, raised at Lissadell House on Sligo Bay.

people.name: Eva Gore-Booth
people.note: Poet, suffragist and labour activist, sister of Constance Markievicz, also raised at Lissadell and remembered in Yeats's verse.

people.name: Michael Coleman
people.note: Fiddler from Killavil whose 1920s and 1930s recordings in New York became the single greatest influence on Irish traditional fiddle playing.

people.name: Shane Filan
people.note: Sligo town native and lead singer of Westlife, the chart-topping boyband formed in Sligo with fellow locals Kian Egan and Mark Feehily.

people.name: Neil Jordan
people.note: Oscar-winning writer and director of The Crying Game and Michael Collins, born in Sligo town in 1950.

people.name: Ray MacSharry
people.note: Sligo politician who served as Tánaiste, Minister for Finance and European Commissioner, nicknamed Mac the Knife for his budget discipline.

people.name: Tommy Fleming
people.note: One of Ireland's best-loved folk and ballad singers, from Aclare in south Sligo.

facts: Carrowmore is one of the largest and oldest megalithic cemeteries in Ireland, with some monuments believed to predate Newgrange.
The huge unexcavated cairn on Knocknarea is reputed to be the grave of Queen Maeve of Connacht, and tradition asks climbers to carry a stone up to add to it.
Three ships of the Spanish Armada were wrecked at Streedagh Strand in 1588, and survivor Francisco de Cuéllar left one of the most vivid first-hand accounts of Armada-era Ireland.
W.B. Yeats won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1923 and lies at Drumcliff beneath the epitaph he wrote himself: cast a cold eye on life, on death.
Sligo's Irish name, Sligeach, means the shelly place, a reference to the shellfish-rich estuary of the Garavogue.
Lord Mountbatten was assassinated by an IRA bomb on his boat off Mullaghmore in August 1979.
Sligo Rovers, playing at the Showgrounds since 1928, are one of the few fully supporter-owned senior football clubs in Ireland.
The Book of Ballymote, compiled in the county around 1391, provided the key that allowed scholars to decipher the ancient ogham alphabet.

intro: They say Cavan has a lake for every day of the year, and the claim is scarcely an exaggeration: the county's drumlin belt is threaded with hundreds of lakes and little hills left behind by the last Ice Age. This is the old heartland of the Gaelic kingdom of East Breifne, ruled by the O'Reillys, whose name still dominates the local phone book and the GAA team sheet. On the slopes of Cuilcagh mountain rises the Shannon Pot, the traditional source of Ireland's longest river, while underground the county shares the Marble Arch Caves Geopark with Fermanagh, the world's first cross-border geopark.

Though part of Ulster, Cavan lies in the Republic, and its border position shaped centuries of plantation, partition and quiet resilience. The land favours small farms, lakes and hedgerows over big fields, and the county's fortunes were built on markets, linen and later engineering and food businesses in towns like Cootehill, Kingscourt and Ballyjamesduff. Cavan people are famed, with a wink, for their thrift, but the county gave generously of its emigrants: from Marcus Daly, the Copper King of Montana, to the thousands whose descendants come back looking for townlands around Belturbet, Bailieborough and Virginia.

towns.name: Cavan
towns.note: The county town, grown around a 14th-century Franciscan friary, with a fine 1940s cathedral and a strong record of hosting the Fleadh Cheoil.

towns.name: Virginia
towns.note: Planned plantation town on Lough Ramor, founded around 1610 and named in honour of Elizabeth I, the Virgin Queen.

towns.name: Ballyjamesduff
towns.note: Market town immortalised in Percy French's song Come Back Paddy Reilly, home to the Cavan County Museum and birthplace of Montana copper magnate Marcus Daly.

towns.name: Cootehill
towns.note: Handsome planter town that prospered on the 18th-century linen trade, named after the Coote family.

towns.name: Belturbet
towns.note: Historic garrison town on the River Erne, now a popular boating base on the Shannon-Erne Waterway.

towns.name: Bailieborough
towns.note: East Cavan market town, birthplace of the pacifist and 1916 martyr Francis Sheehy-Skeffington.

towns.name: Kingscourt
towns.note: Town beside the great gypsum deposits that supply much of the plasterboard used in Irish construction.

towns.name: Ballyconnell
towns.note: Border town at the Cavan end of the restored Shannon-Erne Waterway, in the shadow of Cuilcagh mountain.

people.name: Owen Roe O'Neill

people.name: St Kilian

people.name: Francis Sheehy-Skeffington

people.name: John Charles McQuaid

people.name: T.P. McKenna

people.name: Neven Maguire

facts: The 1947 All-Ireland football final, in which Cavan beat Kerry, was played at the Polo Grounds in New York, the only final ever staged outside Ireland.
The Shannon Pot on the slopes of Cuilcagh is the traditional source of the River Shannon, Ireland's longest river.
Cavan is reputed to contain 365 lakes, one for every day of the year, a legacy of its Ice Age drumlin landscape.
Songwriter Percy French worked in County Cavan as an inspector of drains in the 1880s, and later immortalised Ballyjamesduff in Come Back Paddy Reilly.
The Marble Arch Caves Geopark, shared between Cavan and Fermanagh, became the world's first international cross-border geopark in 2008.

The original Ballinamore-Ballyconnell canal was such a failure that only eight boats paid tolls before it closed; reborn in 1994 as the Shannon-Erne Waterway, it now links Ireland's two great river systems.
The plain of Magh Slécht near Ballyconnell was, according to early Irish texts, the cult centre of the pagan idol Crom Cruach, associated with the carved Killycluggin Stone.
Much of the plasterboard used in Irish building comes from the gypsum deposits mined around Kingscourt.

intro: Wild, remote and fiercely proud of it, Donegal occupies the far north-west of the island, tied to the rest of the Republic by only a narrow strip of land around Bundoran. Its name, Dún na nGall, means 'fort of the foreigners', a nod to the Vikings, but the county's soul is thoroughly Gaelic: the Donegal Gaeltacht is one of the largest Irish-speaking regions in the country, and the distinctive Ulster dialect of Irish still rings out in Gweedore, the Rosses and Cloughaneely. The landscape is the county's calling card — the quartzite cone of Errigal, the sea cliffs of Slieve League, and a shattered Atlantic coastline of headlands, sea loughs and golden strands.

Historically this was the heartland of the O'Donnell clan, whose departure in the 1607 Flight of the Earls from Rathmullan marked the end of the old Gaelic order. Emigration shaped Donegal deeply — seasonal 'tattie hokers' crossed to Scotland for generations, and the county's diaspora stretches from Glasgow to Philadelphia. Its economy rests on fishing out of Killybegs, Ireland's premier fishing port, farming, tourism and the famous handwoven Donegal tweed of Ardara and Kilcar. Traditional music thrives here too, with a driving fiddle style all of its own, exported to the world by Clannad, Enya and Altan.

towns.name: Letterkenny

towns.name: Killybegs

towns.name: Buncrana

towns.name: Bundoran

towns.name: Ballyshannon

towns.name: Ardara

towns.name: Gweedore

towns.name: Dungloe

people.name: Patrick MacGill

people.name: Isaac Butt

facts: Malin Head on the Inishowen Peninsula is the northernmost point of the island of Ireland — yet Donegal lies in the Republic, further north than anywhere in Northern Ireland.
The sea cliffs at Slieve League fall some 600 metres to the Atlantic, making them among the highest accessible sea cliffs in Europe.
Scenes from Star Wars: The Last Jedi were filmed at Malin Head in 2016.
The Flight of the Earls, which ended the Gaelic aristocratic order in Ireland, departed from Rathmullan on Lough Swilly in September 1607.
Glenveagh is one of Ireland's national parks, and its castle was once owned by American art collector Henry McIlhenny, who hosted Greta Garbo there.
Tory Island, nine miles off the coast, maintained the tradition of electing its own 'King of Tory' into the 21st century.
The Grianán of Aileach, a restored stone ringfort on a hilltop overlooking Lough Swilly, was a royal seat of the northern Uí Néill for centuries.
Fanad Head Lighthouse, guarding the mouth of Lough Swilly since 1817, is regularly voted one of the most beautiful lighthouses in the world.

intro: Little hills without end give Monaghan its name — Muineachán derives from the Irish for a place of small hills or thickets — and its distinctive drumlin landscape of rounded knolls, hidden lakes and winding lanes. This is Patrick Kavanagh country: the poet of the 'stony grey soil' grew up farming at Inniskeen, and his clear-eyed, affectionate portrait of small-farm life made Monaghan one of the most vividly written-about counties in Ireland. One of the three Ulster counties in the Republic, Monaghan wraps around the border, and partition cut deeply here, severing railways and hinterlands, especially around the old junction town of Clones.

Monaghan's quiet appearance belies a powerhouse agri-food economy: the county is a national leader in poultry, mushrooms, and furniture-making, with strong family firms exporting across Europe. Its craft heritage is world-class too — Carrickmacross lace and Clones lace, born of famine-relief schemes in the 19th century, adorned royal wedding gowns and are still made by hand today. Gaelic football is a passion bordering on religion, with St Tiernach's Park in Clones long a hallowed venue for Ulster finals, while Castleblayney's country music tradition earned it the nickname of Ireland's Nashville in the era of Big Tom.

towns.name: Emyvale

facts: Carrickmacross lace was incorporated into the wedding dress of Diana, Princess of Wales, in 1981, and lace from the town also featured in later royal wardrobes.
Monaghan is one of only three Ulster counties — with Cavan and Donegal — that remained in the Irish Free State after partition in 1921.
Paul McCartney married Heather Mills at Castle Leslie in Glaslough in 2002, briefly making the quiet estate village world news.
Monaghan farms produce a large share of Ireland's mushrooms and poultry, making the county an agri-food powerhouse out of all proportion to its size.
Gregg shorthand, invented by Rockcorry-born John Robert Gregg, became the standard shorthand system across North America.
Partition devastated Clones as a railway junction: the Great Northern Railway line criss-crossed the new border repeatedly, and services were eventually abandoned in 1957.
The county town's central marketplace, the Diamond, features the ornate Rossmore Memorial, a Victorian drinking fountain that is one of the finest of its kind in Ireland.
Patrick Kavanagh's poem On Raglan Road, set to the air The Dawning of the Day, became one of the most recorded Irish songs of the 20th century.

intro: Few counties pack in as much drama per mile as Antrim. Its northern coast carries the Giant's Causeway, some 40,000 interlocking basalt columns formed by ancient volcanic activity and wrapped in the legend of Finn McCool, while the nine Glens of Antrim sweep green valleys down to the Sea of Moyle, with Scotland's Mull of Kintyre visible barely a dozen miles away. That closeness to Scotland has shaped everything here: the medieval kingdom of Dál Riada spanned the channel, the MacDonnell clan ruled from Dunluce Castle, and Ulster-Scots speech and song remain a living strand of the county's culture alongside its Gaelic and English inheritances.

Antrim's story is also an industrial one. Belfast, which grew along the Antrim side of the Lagan, boomed on linen, rope-making and shipbuilding to become one of the great Victorian industrial cities, and the county's mill towns and market towns — Ballymena, Lisburn, Larne — shared in that prosperity. Today visitors come for the Causeway Coastal Route, one of the world's great drives, for golf at Royal Portrush, whiskey at Bushmills and Game of Thrones filming locations from the Dark Hedges to Ballintoy. A county shared warmly by all traditions, Antrim rewards those tracing Presbyterian, Catholic and Church of Ireland roots alike.

facts: The Giant's Causeway is Northern Ireland's only UNESCO World Heritage Site, formed by volcanic activity around 60 million years ago.
Old Bushmills Distillery traces its licence to distil to 1608, giving it a claim to be the oldest licensed whiskey distillery in the world.
According to tradition, the young St Patrick herded sheep as a slave on Slemish mountain near Ballymena.
A cave on Rathlin Island is reputed to be where Robert the Bruce, in hiding after defeat in 1306, watched the spider that inspired him to try again.
William of Orange landed at Carrickfergus in June 1690 on his way to the Battle of the Boyne.
The Antrim Coast Road, blasted through cliffs in the 1830s to link the isolated Glens, is regarded as one of the great feats of Victorian road engineering.
When the Open Championship came to Royal Portrush in 2019, it was the first time golf's oldest major had been played outside Great Britain since 1951 — also at Portrush.

Lough Neagh, which borders Antrim on the west, is the largest lake in these islands and by legend was formed when Finn McCool scooped out a clod of earth and hurled it into the sea, creating the Isle of Man.

intro: Ireland's ecclesiastical capital for over 1,500 years, Armagh takes its name from Ard Mhacha, the height of Macha, the goddess-queen of Ulster legend. St Patrick chose the hill here for his principal church around 445 AD, and today two St Patrick's Cathedrals — Church of Ireland and Roman Catholic — face each other across the small Georgian city, each the seat of an all-Ireland primate. Two miles west stands Navan Fort, Emain Macha, the ancient capital of the Kings of Ulster and setting of the Táin sagas, making this compact county a place of extraordinary depth for anyone tracing the deep roots of Irish identity.

Beyond the city, Armagh is the Orchard County: apple growing was recorded here well over a millennium ago, and the pink-and-white blossom of May around Loughgall and Richhill remains a glorious sight, with the Armagh Bramley apple now protected under EU designation. Linen once powered towns like Lurgan, Portadown and the Quaker model village of Bessbrook, while today the county is renowned for Gaelic football — Crossmaglen Rangers are among the most decorated clubs in Ireland — and for road bowls, the ancient sport of hurling an iron bullet along country lanes, kept alive here and in Cork. Visitors of every tradition find a shared heritage in its cathedrals, orchards and observatory.

facts: Armagh is the ecclesiastical capital of all Ireland: both the Catholic Church and the Church of Ireland seat their all-island primates in the city.
Navan Fort, or Emain Macha, was the royal capital of ancient Ulster and features in the epic tales of Cú Chulainn and the Red Branch Knights.
Armagh Observatory, founded in 1790, holds one of the longest continuous series of daily weather records anywhere in the world, unbroken since 1795.
The Armagh Bramley apple holds EU Protected Geographical Indication status, and apple growing in the county was recorded more than a thousand years ago.
Armagh is the smallest of the six counties of Northern Ireland by area.
Road bowls, in which players hurl a 28-ounce iron bullet along winding country roads in as few throws as possible, survives almost exclusively in Armagh and Cork.
The Bessbrook and Newry Tramway, opened in 1885, was one of the first hydroelectric-powered railways in the world.
Ireland's oldest public library outside Dublin, the Armagh Robinson Library of 1771, holds Jonathan Swift's own annotated copy of Gulliver's Travels.

intro: Few places in Ireland carry as much history within so small a compass as Derry, whose county town remains the only completely walled city on the island. The walls, raised between 1613 and 1619 during the Plantation of Ulster, were never breached — hence the nickname the Maiden City — and today you can walk their full circuit above the Bogside and the Guildhall. Beyond the city, the county unfolds into the heathery Sperrin Mountains, the fertile Roe and Faughan valleys, and a magnificent Atlantic coastline at Downhill, Castlerock and Portstewart, where the clifftop Mussenden Temple has become one of the most photographed buildings in Ireland.

Derry earned its living for generations from shirt-making — by the late nineteenth century it was one of the great shirt-producing centres of the world, an industry that famously employed far more women than men. The county's cultural weight is remarkable: Seamus Heaney grew up on a farm at Mossbawn near Bellaghy, and his poetry is saturated with this landscape of flax dams, bog and blackberries. In 2013 Derry-Londonderry became the first ever UK City of Culture, and the Peace Bridge across the Foyle, opened in 2011, has become a symbol of a city and county looking forward while honouring both of its traditions.

facts: Derry's city walls, completed in 1619, are the only complete city walls in Ireland and were never breached, earning Derry the title of the Maiden City.
The Siege of Derry in 1689 lasted 105 days and is remembered as the longest siege in British and Irish history.
Amelia Earhart landed in a field at Ballyarnett just outside Derry in 1932, completing the first solo transatlantic flight by a woman.
The melody of Danny Boy, known as the Londonderry Air, was collected in Limavady in the 1850s by Jane Ross.
The name Derry comes from the Irish Doire, meaning oak grove, recalling the wood where St Colmcille founded his monastery.
In the nineteenth century Derry was one of the shirt-making capitals of the world, and its factories were even mentioned by Karl Marx in Das Kapital.
Mountsandel near Coleraine has evidence of habitation from around 7600 BC, among the oldest known human settlement sites in Ireland.
Derry-Londonderry was named the first ever UK City of Culture in 2013, marked by the opening of the curved Peace Bridge across the Foyle in 2011.

intro: Where the Mountains of Mourne sweep down to the sea — Percy French's famous line describes County Down exactly, for the granite Mournes rise almost straight from the beach at Newcastle, crowned by Slieve Donard, Northern Ireland's highest peak at 850 metres. This is also St Patrick's county: he is said to have begun his Irish mission at Saul near Downpatrick in 432 and to lie buried beside Down Cathedral. Between the mountains and Belfast Lough stretches a gentle drumlin landscape, the island-speckled waters of Strangford Lough, and the long arm of the Ards Peninsula, dotted with fishing harbours and early Christian sites.

Down has long been prosperous farming and market-town country, its northern edge now woven into Belfast's commuter belt through Holywood, Bangor and Comber. Its people have shaped the wider world out of all proportion to its size: Hans Sloane of Killyleagh founded the collection that became the British Museum, Thomas Andrews of Comber designed the Titanic, and Harry Ferguson from near Dromore revolutionised world farming with his tractor system. Golf pilgrims come for Royal County Down at Newcastle, walkers for the Mourne Wall and Tollymore Forest, and family historians for the graveyards and meeting houses that record centuries of both Planter and Gael.

towns.name: Portaferry
towns.note: A harbour town on the fast-flowing Strangford Narrows, reached by ferry and home to the Exploris aquarium.

towns.name: Holywood
towns.note: A seaside town on Belfast Lough famous for its maypole and as the home town of golfer Rory McIlroy.

towns.name: Banbridge
towns.note: A linen-era town on the River Bann whose unusual sunken carriageway, the Cut, was built in 1834 to help mail coaches up the steep main street.

towns.name: Warrenpoint
towns.note: A Victorian resort on Carlingford Lough looking across to the Cooley Mountains, with a summer ferry to Omeath.

towns.name: Killyleagh
towns.note: A village on Strangford Lough dominated by a turreted castle and known as the birthplace of Sir Hans Sloane.

people.name: St Patrick
people.note: Ireland's patron saint began his mission at Saul near Downpatrick in 432 and is reputedly buried at Down Cathedral.

people.name: Sir Hans Sloane
people.note: Killyleagh-born physician and collector whose vast collection founded the British Museum and who popularised drinking chocolate.

people.name: Thomas Andrews
people.note: The Comber-born naval architect who designed the Titanic and went down with the ship in 1912.

people.name: Harry Ferguson
people.note: Born near Dromore, he made the first powered flight in Ireland in 1909 and transformed world agriculture with the Ferguson tractor system.

people.name: Patrick Bronte
people.note: Father of the Bronte novelists, born in a cottage at Drumballyroney near Rathfriland before making his way to Cambridge and Yorkshire.

people.name: Francis Crozier
people.note: Banbridge-born polar explorer who commanded HMS Terror and vanished with the Franklin expedition in the Arctic.

people.name: Rory McIlroy
people.note: Holywood's four-time major champion golfer, who completed the career Grand Slam at the 2025 Masters.

people.name: Jamie Dornan
people.note: Holywood-born actor known for The Fall, Fifty Shades of Grey and Belfast.

people.name: James Martin
people.note: Engineer from Crossgar whose Martin-Baker ejection seats have saved thousands of pilots' lives.

facts: Slieve Donard, at 850 metres, is the highest mountain in Northern Ireland, and the 35-kilometre dry-stone Mourne Wall crosses fifteen summits around it.
The Newry Canal, opened in 1742, was the first summit-level canal in Britain or Ireland, predating England's celebrated Bridgewater Canal.
The Antiphonary of Bangor, written at Bangor Abbey in the seventh century, is one of the oldest surviving Irish manuscripts and is now kept in Milan.
Strangford Lough is the largest sea inlet in Britain and Ireland, and in 2008 its narrows hosted SeaGen, the world's first large-scale commercial tidal stream turbine.
Hillsborough Castle is the official residence of the monarch in Northern Ireland and hosted key negotiations throughout the peace process.
Royal County Down at Newcastle is regularly ranked among the greatest golf courses in the world.
The name Down comes from the Irish Dun, meaning fort, after the great hilltop fort at Downpatrick.
Tollymore Forest Park near Newcastle, opened in 1955, was the first state forest park in Northern Ireland and later served as a filming location for Game of Thrones.

intro: Water defines Fermanagh more than any other Irish county: roughly a third of it lies under lakes and rivers, and locals like to say that for six months of the year Lough Erne is in Fermanagh, and for the other six Fermanagh is in Lough Erne. The county town of Enniskillen sits on an island in the river between Upper and Lower Lough Erne, a natural fortress that made it the seat of the Maguire chieftains, who ruled Fermanagh for centuries and patrolled the lakes with a private fleet of boats. Scattered across the waters are islands rich in carved stones and monastic ruins, from the round tower of Devenish to the enigmatic Janus figure on Boa Island.

Away from the loughs, Fermanagh rises into limestone uplands riddled with caves — the Marble Arch Caves near Florencecourt anchor a UNESCO Global Geopark that reaches across the border into Cavan. This is a county of stately homes such as Castle Coole and Florence Court, of the delicate Parian china made at Belleek since 1857, and of quiet market villages where anglers and boaters set out onto some of the best coarse fishing waters in Europe. Portora Royal School in Enniskillen educated both Oscar Wilde and Samuel Beckett, and in 2013 the eyes of the world turned to the Lough Erne Resort when it hosted the G8 summit.

towns.name: Enniskillen
towns.note: The county town, built on an island between Upper and Lower Lough Erne and guarded by the Maguires' castle.

towns.name: Lisnaskea
towns.note: Fermanagh's second town, close to the crowning place of the Maguire chieftains at Cornashee.

towns.name: Belleek
towns.note: One of the most westerly villages in Northern Ireland, world-famous for the Parian china produced at Belleek Pottery since 1857.

towns.name: Irvinestown
towns.note: A Plantation market town near Necarne Castle and the wartime flying-boat base at Castle Archdale.

towns.name: Kesh
towns.note: A village at the top of Lower Lough Erne popular with anglers and the gateway to Boa Island's ancient carved figures.

towns.name: Belcoo
towns.note: A border village facing Blacklion in Cavan across the water, set between the two Lough Macneans.

towns.name: Garrison
towns.note: A small angling village on Lough Melvin, a lake famous for its unique native trout varieties.

towns.name: Newtownbutler
towns.note: A border village in south Fermanagh near the reedy islands and waterways of Upper Lough Erne.

towns.name: Derrygonnelly
towns.note: A village beneath the cliffs of Magho, a gateway to the walking country of the western Fermanagh uplands.

people.name: The Maguires
people.note: The Gaelic dynasty that ruled Fermanagh from the thirteenth to the seventeenth century, giving the county its enduring identity.

people.name: Oscar Wilde
people.note: The playwright spent his schooldays at Portora Royal School in Enniskillen in the 1860s and early 1870s.

people.name: Samuel Beckett
people.note: The Nobel laureate boarded at Portora Royal School in Enniskillen, where he excelled at cricket as much as at books.

people.name: Adrian Dunbar
people.note: Enniskillen-born actor and director best known as Superintendent Ted Hastings in Line of Duty.

people.name: Neil Hannon
people.note: The Divine Comedy songwriter grew up in Enniskillen, where his father was the Church of Ireland Bishop of Clogher.

people.name: Joan Trimble
people.note: Enniskillen-born pianist and composer who, with her sister Valerie, formed a celebrated piano duo in the mid-twentieth century.

people.name: Frank Ormsby
people.note: Poet and long-time anthologist of Ulster writing, born in Enniskillen and raised in rural Fermanagh.

people.name: Kyle Lafferty
people.note: Footballer from Kesh who scored crucial goals in Northern Ireland's run to Euro 2016.

people.name: Ciaran McMenamin
people.note: Enniskillen-born actor and novelist known for David Copperfield and Primeval.

facts: About a third of County Fermanagh is covered by water, the highest proportion of any Irish county.
Enniskillen's historic core stands on an island in the River Erne, making it unique among Irish county towns.
The Marble Arch Caves form the heart of a UNESCO Global Geopark that was the first in the world to span an international border, reaching into County Cavan.
Belleek Pottery, founded in 1857, is one of Ireland's oldest working potteries and its delicate Parian china is prized by collectors worldwide.
The two-faced Janus figure on Boa Island is one of the most mysterious stone carvings in Ireland, possibly dating from the Iron Age.
The Lough Erne Resort outside Enniskillen hosted the G8 summit of world leaders in June 2013.
Fermanagh has had no railway since 1957, when the Great Northern lines through the county were closed.
During the Second World War, Catalina and Sunderland flying boats patrolled the Atlantic from bases on Lough Erne, using a secret flight corridor over neutral Donegal.

intro: Tyrone is the largest of Northern Ireland's six counties, a broad inland sweep of glens, bog and farmland rising to the Sperrin Mountains along its northern rim. Its name, Tir Eoghain, means the land of Eoghan, a son of Niall of the Nine Hostages, and for centuries it was the heartland of the O'Neills, the most powerful Gaelic dynasty in Ireland. Hugh O'Neill, Earl of Tyrone, led the great Gaelic resistance of the Nine Years' War before sailing from Ireland in 1607 in the Flight of the Earls — the event that opened the door to the Plantation of Ulster and reshaped the province forever.

Few counties are as bound up with the story of emigration to America. The Ulster American Folk Park outside Omagh grew around the boyhood home of Thomas Mellon, founder of the Pittsburgh banking dynasty, and the ancestral homesteads of Presidents Ulysses S. Grant and Woodrow Wilson still stand at Ballygawley and near Strabane. Strabane itself was a famous printing town whose apprentice John Dunlap went on to print the American Declaration of Independence. Today Tyrone is known for its engineering firms, its lively market towns, the Bronze Age mystery of the Beaghmore stone circles, and a fierce devotion to Gaelic football that has brought Sam Maguire home four times.

towns.name: Omagh
towns.note: The county town at the meeting of the Drumragh and Camowen rivers, with the Ulster American Folk Park on its doorstep.

towns.name: Dungannon
towns.note: The historic seat of the O'Neill chieftains, whose castle hill overlooks a town later built on linen and engineering.

towns.name: Strabane
towns.note: A border town with a famous printing tradition — John Dunlap and James Wilson, grandfather of President Woodrow Wilson, both learned their trades here.

towns.name: Cookstown
towns.note: A Plantation town famous for its main street, around two kilometres long and one of the longest in Ireland.

towns.name: Coalisland
towns.note: A former coal-mining and canal town, and the home of 1985 world snooker champion Dennis Taylor.

towns.name: Castlederg
towns.note: A west Tyrone market town on the River Derg whose castle ruins recall centuries of border warfare.

towns.name: Sion Mills
towns.note: A picturesque model village built around a great linen spinning mill by the Herdman family in the 1830s.

towns.name: Clogher
towns.note: A tiny cathedral town in a fertile valley, seat of one of the oldest bishoprics in Ireland.

towns.name: Benburb
towns.note: A village above the Blackwater gorge, site of Owen Roe O'Neill's famous victory over a Covenanter army in 1646.

towns.name: Moy
towns.note: An elegant village laid out in the 1760s by Lord Charlemont, reputedly on the plan of an Italian piazza, and once famed for its horse fairs.

people.name: Hugh O'Neill
people.note: Earl of Tyrone and last great Gaelic lord of Ireland, who led the Nine Years' War and departed in the Flight of the Earls in 1607.

people.name: John Dunlap
people.note: Strabane-born printer who printed the first copies of the American Declaration of Independence and founded America's first successful daily newspaper.

people.name: Flann O'Brien (Brian O'Nolan)
people.note: The comic novelist behind At Swim-Two-Birds and The Third Policeman was born in Strabane in 1911.

people.name: Brian Friel
people.note: One of Ireland's greatest playwrights, author of Translations and Dancing at Lughnasa, born near Omagh in 1929.

people.name: Benedict Kiely
people.note: Novelist, broadcaster and seanchai of modern Irish letters, raised in Omagh, which colours much of his fiction.

people.name: Jimmy Kennedy
people.note: Omagh-born songwriter whose hits included Teddy Bears' Picnic and Red Sails in the Sunset.

people.name: Dennis Taylor
people.note: Coalisland-born snooker player who won the 1985 world championship on the final black in front of 18.5 million BBC viewers.

people.name: Darren Clarke
people.note: Dungannon golfer who won the Open Championship in 2011 and starred in multiple Ryder Cups.

people.name: Peter Canavan
people.note: Ballygawley Gaelic footballer regarded as one of the greatest ever, who captained Tyrone to their first All-Ireland title in 2003.

facts: Tyrone is the largest county in Northern Ireland, covering more than 3,200 square kilometres from Lough Neagh to the Donegal border.
The Beaghmore stone circles near Cookstown, uncovered during turf cutting in the 1940s, comprise seven circles and dozens of cairns and alignments from the Bronze Age.
John Dunlap of Strabane printed the Declaration of Independence on the night of 4 July 1776, and the surviving copies are known as Dunlap broadsides.
The ancestral homes of two US presidents survive in Tyrone: Ulysses S. Grant's at Ballygawley and Woodrow Wilson's family homestead at Dergalt near Strabane.
The Ulster American Folk Park at Omagh grew around the cottage where Thomas Mellon, founder of the Mellon banking dynasty of Pittsburgh, was born in 1813.
The name Tyrone comes from Tir Eoghain, the land of Eoghan, a son of the legendary fifth-century king Niall of the Nine Hostages.
Tyrone have won the All-Ireland Senior Football Championship four times, in 2003, 2005, 2008 and 2021.
Cookstown was laid out with a main street around two kilometres long, often cited as the longest in Ireland, earning it the nickname the Long Line.
